item.title: [roundtable.io] Muncy Delivers Resilient Season as Dodgers’ Longest-Tenured Player
item.dc:creator: Anthony Arroyo

item.content:encoded:
Max Muncy remained a key contributor for the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2026, while establishing himself as one of the club’s most experienced leaders.
With Clayton Kershaw retiring, Muncy became the longest-tenured player on the Dodgers’ roster, taking on an even more prominent place within the organization. The veteran infielder responded with one of his most productive seasons.
Muncy appeared in 149 games during the 2026 regular season, establishing a new career high. He finished with a .252 batting average, a .348 on-base percentage, and a .490 slugging percentage, recording 29 home runs and 76 RBIs.
Muncy makes Dodger Stadium history
One of Muncy’s biggest accomplishments in 2026 came at the ballpark he has called home since joining the Dodgers in 2018.
He later surpassed Eric Karros for the most career home runs at Dodger Stadium, adding another milestone to his accomplishments with the franchise.
The record further cemented Muncy’s place in Dodgers history. Although he has experienced stretches of inconsistency and dealt with criticism of his defense at third base, his offensive contributions have made him an important part of the team’s success over multiple seasons.
Postseason success gives way to NLCS struggles
Muncy carried his power into the postseason, helping the Dodgers generate offense against the Atlanta Braves in the National League Division Series. He hit three home runs during the series, providing a significant boost as Los Angeles advanced.
Muncy remains part of Dodgers’ plans
Muncy’s contract situation also gives the Dodgers a clearer picture of their immediate future. His 2026 playing-time milestones reportedly triggered incentives, increasing his earnings for the season and raising his guaranteed 2027 salary to $10.75 million. The club also holds a $10 million option for 2028, with a $3 million buyout.
As he approaches his age-36 season, questions about durability and long-term production will naturally follow. Still, his availability and power in 2026 demonstrated that he can remain a productive contributor.
With his experience, franchise history, and continued presence in the lineup, Muncy is expected to remain an important veteran for Los Angeles in 2027. His latest campaign reinforced his value to the Dodgers, even as the team faces the challenge of keeping its veteran core healthy and productive.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Max Muncy compares Tarik Skubal to Clayton Kershaw on start days
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Abdón Ibarra

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers took a big swing at the trade deadline to acquire Tarik Skubal, and although they fell short of a three-peat, the left-hander was instrumental to success they did have in the meantime.
Not only was Skubal extremely valuable on the mound, but he also become a popular figure in the clubhouse. Part of that stems from how Skubal interacted with his teammates, even on days when he was the starting pitcher.
But how Skubal presents himself now was not always the case during his career. Instead, he often emulated behavior he saw from veterans in the Detroit Tigers’ clubhouse. That typically involved having headphones in and keeping to themselves. But at a certain point, he decided it would be more beneficial to be his authentic self instead.
“I just found it to be exhausting. I don’t think that’s who I am. It’s kind of putting on a facade,” Skubal recently explained. “You’re just not yourself. I didn’t feel like myself when I was doing that, putting headphones in and trying to be focused. I found myself mentally exhausted in the second or third innings of games.
“And I’m like, ‘Why am I tired today? I should be ready to go.’ When I got hurt in ’22, I decided enough is enough. I’m caring way too much about all the little things that don’t really matter, don’t really impact the game of baseball.
“I don’t know if it’s like superstitious, but like making sure the music is the right setting, making sure the music is the right songs at the right time, and you’re just caring about all the wrong things, I think. For me it was mentally freeing to take my headphones off and just be who I am and interact with guys.
“As it gets closer to game time, you get ready to go and you’re going to go out there and compete. But I just didn’t really find much of a benefit of trying to be locked in four hours before a game. I want to be myself. Then I’ll lock in as the game gets closer.”
Max Muncy compares Tarik Skubal to Clayton Kershaw
For the Dodgers players who have been around awhile, including Max Muncy, Skubal’s approach represented a drastic departure from what they would normally see from a pitcher like Clayton Kershaw.
“For me with starting pitchers, when it’s their start day, it’s always kind of an interesting debacle, we’ll call it,” Muncy began when asked about Skubal’s demeanor.
“With him, I’ve never seen somebody be so normal on a start day. To me that’s really refreshing and really awesome to see. He doesn’t change his attitude or his mind, the way he acts in the clubhouse with the other guys. For a guy to be as competitive as he is on the mound and as fiery as he is, it’s really awesome to see how he goes about every other day exactly the same. That’s pretty rare to see.”
Muncy noticed a difference between the two pitchers from Skubal’s first start for the Dodgers.
“[Skubal] came up to me and started asking me questions and talking about something that wasn’t even involved in the game. I don’t remember what it was, but he was talking about something and it just completely threw me off,” Muncy recalled. “Like you said, playing with Kersh for all those years, it’s the complete opposite.
“That’s where I go to the word ‘debacle’ a bit. Us position players always laugh about the starting pitchers just because could you imagine if we acted that way every time we had to start on the field? Those are the main guys. They have their routines, and they’re that way for a reason. You can’t win games without them.
“So you really need the starting pitching. Whatever routine they want to go with and whatever show they want to put on, we’re here for all of it. Yeah, Scoobs and Kersh couldn’t be more opposite in terms of their start day routine.”

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers 2026 report card: Shohei Ohtani gets an F, only two hitters receive an A
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers won 100 games this season. They claimed the National League West division yet again. But, after reaching the National League Championship Series, their World Series three-peat bid flamed out in a sweep to the Brewers.
In the wake of their elimination, The California Post graded the season of every player on the Dodgers’ roster.
First up, the offense, which ranked top-five in the regular season in scoring, batting average and OPS –– but faltered in the playoffs and was shut down in the NLCS.
Shohei Ohtani: F
To be clear: The two-way star was the second-best player in the National League this year, hitting 30 home runs and posting a sub-2.00 ERA in 14 starts on the mound. Even in a relatively down year for him, he finished fifth in the majors in Fangraphs’ version of wins above replacement. He remains, undoubtedly, MLB’s foremost star player and the Dodgers’ most potent weapon.
But that is why the way his season finished was such a failure.
What mattered most for the Dodgers this year was having Ohtani –– especially as a hitter –– at full strength come the postseason. By trying to play through right arm and left knee injuries, he wasn’t.
And while there is blame to be shared for the way his health was managed, from team decision-makers to Ohtani himself, it is impossible not to second-guess what this October might have looked like if the slugger was in a better place physically.
Instead, his .192 playoff batting average was not nearly enough to save the Dodgers’ offense. In the end, his one big swing in Game 4 of the NLCS was too little, too late. Moving forward, he and the team might have to reimagine his usage to avoid a repeat of this year. Because, especially as the rest of the roster gets older, they can’t afford another late-season injury crisis like this with Ohtani again.
Freddie Freeman: B-
In his 17th MLB season, Freeman earned his 10th career All-Star selection, finished 13th in the majors in total hits, and continued his march towards Cooperstown. But, the 37-year-old also saw his total production (measured by WAR) decline for a fourth-straight year.
He hit just one regular-season home run after July 4. His batting average dropped from .306 to .288 amid a knee issue in September. And despite a couple big swings in the playoffs, he finished October just 5-for-29. Now, entering the final season of his contract but intending to play at least a couple more beyond that, the Dodgers will have to start deciding if he will remain in their longer-term plans.
Mookie Betts: B
What was shaping up to be a lost year for Betts instead finished with signs of renewed life. On Aug. 4, he was hitting .223 with a .670 OPS. In 46 games after that, he posted a .315/.399/.562 slash line while nearly doubling his home run total from 13 to 23.
It was the best he had looked since the first half of 2024 and a reminder that, even at 34 years old now, there is a superstar level he is still capable of reaching. The Dodgers will be hoping that’s what they get from him in 2027.
Max Muncy: B+
This was a resurgent season for Muncy, who returned to the All-Star Game for the first time since 2021 while hitting for his highest average (.252) since 2018. He stayed healthy, playing 149 games and hitting 29 home runs.
He also improved his defense, earning a nod as a Gold Glove finalist at third base. He’ll be back at third next season, in the final guaranteed year of his contract.
Andy Pages: A-
Pages didn’t sustain his torrid pace from early in the year (he had a .303 average and .899 OPS on May 27, then a .254 average and .751 OPS thereafter) but still cemented himself as the youngest core piece of the roster, earning an All-Star nod with his improved approach and stellar center-field defense. His postseason was an improvement from 2025 too.
Teoscar Hernández: C
A late surge at the plate helped save some of Hernández’s season-long numbers (.267 average, .759 OPS) following a prolonged slump upon his return from a hamstring strain.
But after being bandied around in potential trade discussions last offseason, it’s possible his future with the club could be in question again this winter.
Kyle Tucker: D
The only thing saving this from being an F is the way Tucker finished his otherwise dismal debut season, highlighted by a team-best .333 batting average in the playoffs. Still, the 29-year-old played nowhere near expectations after his $240 offseason signing, setting career-lows in average (.233), OPS (.715) and home runs (17).
The Dodgers will be desperate for him to return to form next year, when he will play an even more vital role in their still-aging lineup. If not, those $60 million player options in 2028 and 2029 will start to feel like poison pills.
Will Smith: C
This is a relatively incomplete grade, given Smith was limited to just 73 games by a three-month neck injury. But even when he did play, the veteran backstop took a step back. His .260 average and .781 OPS were the second-lowest marks of his career (ahead of only 2024). He went just 3-for-31 in the playoffs, salvaging only so much with his Game 3 double in the NLCS.
Tommy Edman: C
After missing the start of the year recovering from ankle surgery, Edman did little more than meet expectations in his utility role with the Dodgers. He was a streaky .247 hitter, finishing with a just-about-league-average .714 OPS. He played good defense and shifted around the diamond. But any more profound impact was limited.
Kiké Hernández: C
Injuries derailed Hernández’s year. And though he had another big October moment –– hitting a home run off Chris Sale in the NLDS –– there was little else to take from his 13th big-league campaign. Once again a free agent, he will represent one of the more intriguing questions of the Dodgers’ winter.
Each of the last three offseasons, they have re-signed him to a one-year deal. Whether they do so again could be a signal for how much, or little, of a shake-up they’re planning for next year.
Dalton Rushing: B
For Rushing, it was a year of promising highs (seven home runs in March/April, .288 batting average in July) and frustrating lows (emotional outbursts early in the year, his spat with Ohtani on the mound in June, and a late-season elbow injury that sidelined him for the playoffs) for the former top prospect. He has more to prove entering Year 3 in 2027.
Alex Freeland: C
Another ex-prospect, Freeland didn’t capitalize on increased opportunity this year, hitting just .234 with only 13 extra-base hits in 89 games. Though still only 25, he remains on the fringes of the team’s long-term plans.
Alex Call: C
The backup outfielder survived the trade deadline. But after hitting just .233 in his reserve role, he might not be a lock to return in his reserve role next year.
Josue De Paula: B+
In his brief MLB debut, De Paula did everything right as a hitter, reaching base at a .500 clip in 11 regular-season games before drawing two key walks as a pinch-hitter in October. Offensively, he seems ready for everyday big-league duties. But the gigantic question mark about his outfield defense leaves his 2027 role unclear entering the winter.
Hyeseong Kim: D
Time will tell if the Dodgers still see something in Kim. But the way he was buried in triple-A this year, after playing just 43 games in the majors in April and May, was not a good sign as he enters the final guaranteed year of his contract.
Hunter Feduccia: B
The former Dodgers farmhand returned to the club in a deadline day trade and was perfectly adequate as the backup catcher over the final couple months of the season. Whether there’s a role for him in the organization again next year remains to be seen.
Miguel Rojas: A
We’re grading on a curve here, in what was a fittingly effective send-off season for the now-retired veteran infielder. Rojas did his job by menacing left-handed pitching (.293 average against them), playing stout defense and serving as a vocal leader in the Dodgers’ star-studded clubhouse. After an accomplished 13-year MLB career –– highlighted by his season-saving home run in Game 7 of last year’s World Series –– his presence will be missed in the clubhouse.

item.content:encoded:
By MIKEY HIRANO CULROSS
Rafu Sports Editor
Shohei Ohtani flung his bat into the air, exulted toward the sky, and for one shining moment, the improbable seemed more than merely possible.
The ball hadn’t yet landed in the right-field pavilion, but the Dodgers and their fans were in full-tilt celebration. Not just because their superstar had hit a home run, but it was a sign that the team’s offensive malaise might finally be breaking, that for the first time in the series, the ball would be bouncing their way.
The notion of a three-peat for the back-to-back world champs was still alive, regardless of the long odds. At this moment, the team many expected to return to the World Series – and win it – appeared to be returning to form.
The joy was a distant memory by the time Kiké Hernandez’ fly ball settled into left-fielder Jackson Chourio’s glove for the final out of the ninth inning on Thursday, as the Milwaukee Brewers swept the Dodgers in the National League Championship Series and booked their first trip to the World Series since 1982.
In perhaps returning the favor from last year, when the Dodgers won four straight against the Brewers, Milwaukee was the better team in essentially every aspect of the game: starting pitching, relief pitching, batting, situational hitting … they simply played winning baseball.
“They played flawless. They really did,” Dodger manager Dave Roberts said in the postgame press conference, after the visiting Brewers overcame a 4-0 deficit and scored six unanswered runs to complete the sweep.
“I think for me, it never feels good to lose, but when you get beat, you can handle it a little bit better,” Roberts said after addressing his team following the loss. “I had a good conversation with the guys in there, and just told them how proud I was. I’m not used to those speeches, those consolation speeches.”
The Brewers had the best record in the major leagues this season, winning 103 games, while L.A. was runner-up with 100 victories.
“For us, it was just pitting two really good ball clubs against one another, and they won out,” Roberts added.
Ohtani’s three-run shot in the second inning was the sole home run of the series for the Dodgers, who had relied heavily on the long ball for wins late in the regular season and into the playoffs.
“I’m very disappointed, but the Brewers are a very good team; you have to give them credit,” Ohtani said through an interpreter in the home clubhouse. “They were able to expose some of our weaknesses.”
For Ohtani, the weaknesses weren’t just stats on a page. He’s been dealing with power-sapping infirmities for months, including a sore right shoulder and gimpy left knee. His last home run came nearly two months prior to Thursday’s shot, and the team shut down his pitching game at the end of July.
He said he is completely committed to returning as a two-way player in 2027, using the off-season to focus on rest, rehab and recovery.
In this year’s NLCS, Ohtani finished batting a paltry .192 with only one home run and 10 strikeouts in 26 at-bats. He had struggled atthe plate to the point there was talk of the unthinkable – Roberts not him starting in Game 4.
After some serious conversation, the manager went with his superstar in the lineup, and early on, at least, it paid off.
“I’ll always trust Shohei. I think he’s the best player on the planet, and he’s not completely healthy,” Roberts explained. “I just give him a lot of respect for not running from it, still wanting to participate, still wanting to play when he’s not 100 percent.”
Roberts noted the rare display of emotion from the Japanese star once the Game 4 home run ball left his bat.
“It was something that you don’t see very often from Shohei. I think it was a lot of pent-up anger, frustration. It was the best ball he hit in probably two, three months, and it was a big hit.
“So I think that for him to look at the dugout, show that emotion, it just shows how much he cares. He’s still human. He still cares and wants to help his team win a baseball game. That was a big hit.”
As gracious as Roberts, Ohtani and the rest of the Dodgers were in defeat, the sting was clear in their voices.
“I’m tremendously grateful for the time we have spent as a team, even though we fell short this year,” Ohtani said. “I want to use this feeling as a catalyst for next season.”
Max Muncy, whose frustrations were laid bare in Game 4 after he struck out with a tying run at third base and slammed his bat to the ground, said he and the Dodgers gave it their best.
“We left it all out there, but the train finally ran out of steam,” Muncy conceded.
The Dodgers were vying to become the first National League team to win three straight World Series titles. The New York Yankees achieved from 1998 to 2000, following the Oakland A’s from 1972 to 1974.
“I certainly think that I wish it was us going to the World Series and defending our crown, but those guys, they earned it, and it’s going to be a heck of a World Series,” Roberts said.
Heading into Game 3 in the American League Championship Series, the Cleveland Guardians held a 2-1 lead over the Tampa Bay Rays. The game scheduled for Friday has been pushed back to Saturday due to weather.
The Brewers and Rays are among the five MLB teams that have never won a World Series, along with the San Diego Padres, Seattle Mariners and Colorado Rockies.

item.title: [dailybulletin.com] Analysis: Dodgers’ NLCS defeat raises questions about team’s aging core
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The past two years, the Dodgers’ season ended with parades and calls to “Run it back” for the next season.
After their four-game sweep in the National League Championship Series at the hands of a younger, hungrier Milwaukee Brewers team ended the dream of a ‘three-peat,’ how realistic is it to head into 2027 with the same core – the oldest position player group in MLB for the past four years?
“That’s not my job. I play first base,” said Freddie Freeman, at 37 the oldest returning player on the Dodgers’ roster (infielder Miguel Rojas announced his retirement and relief pitcher Blake Treinen, who suffered a shoulder injury late in the season, is a free agent).
“We’ve got a great group of guys. We’ve accomplished a lot of things. We came up short in these four days. But we’ll see where the wind blows this offseason, what happens, what it looks like, what baseball looks like.”
The winds of change could be coming. As Freeman alluded to, the anticipated showdown between MLB’s owners and the players’ union over the next Collective Bargaining Agreement could force the biggest changes in the Dodgers’ future. If the owners are able to get the salary cap or other payroll restrictions they are aiming for, the Dodgers might be forced to change their roster by shedding payroll.
Also looming over the team’s future are the ongoing legal and financial difficulties surrounding principal owner Mark Walter that threaten to eat into the Dodgers’ enormous financial advantages.
Threatening the franchise’s plans to keep its “Golden Era” going more directly, though, is the aging roster. The Brewers certainly made the Dodgers look old in the four-game NLCS sweep.
“I don’t know what you can really say to that. That’s just people’s opinions of what that is,” Freeman said before Game 4. “We do know we have an older team. That doesn’t mean we’re old and we’re playing bad because we’re old. We’re just not playing that great, in my mind.
“But that’s people’s opinions. I can’t change your opinion because we are, in this game, a little bit older than everybody else. I don’t feel old.”
Nonetheless, Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman acknowledged awareness – if not overt concern – about the aging core on the team’s roster.
“Yeah, we’ve talked about this a lot,” Friedman said before the start of the NLCS. “With where we are in the success cycle, the success we have had, we have done the opposite of being flippant about it. ‘Oh, it’s great that we won. Now we can put our feet up.’ For us, it’s about pressing the advantage we have right now.
“We have a very talented core, and while a good number of them are getting up there in years, the experience, the way they prepare, the way they play the game, we feel like is a real competitive advantage. So we’ve been aggressive to supplement around that group, all the while pouring ourselves into our next wave.”
The Dodgers’ farm system is indeed as strong as any in MLB. They subtracted two Top 100 prospects (outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-hander River Ryan) in order to trade for pitcher Tarik Skubal in August and still have five more led by outfielder Josue De Paula.
De Paula made the jump from Double-A to the majors in September and showed his readiness in that brief audition. The Dodgers will have to make room for him in their 2027 plan.
That won’t be easy and it’s difficult to see how the Dodgers can get younger in 2027 other than around the margins where Kiké Hernandez acknowledged Game 4 of the NLCS might be his last with the Dodgers and Rojas made it clear, talking to the team after the game and saying he was retiring. He is expected to stay with the organization in some capacity, likely in player development.
“This is it as a player. That was my last game playing. That was the last time I put these cleats on and this uniform on as a player,” Rojas said, still in full uniform long after the game ended Thursday night. “From now on, I’m going to start thinking about what’s going to happen in my life as a baseball person other than being a player. I want to start my career on the other side of this business, and I’m looking forward to doing it here with the Los Angeles Dodgers as well.
“I’m ready to move on and start the next chapter of my career.”
Hernandez isn’t ready to stop playing. But he knows it might not be in Los Angeles next year.
“I mean, I love this place. I’ve played for three other teams, but every time I look at my career I kind of obviously go back to this place,” the 35-year-old Hernandez said. “I feel like I have a lot left. … I would love to be back. I would love to have one more try, trying to win another one. But I don’t really know what’s going to happen. I hope I’m back, and if I’m not I hope that I get to play for a winning team.”
Seven other Dodgers will become free agents this winter, most prominently bullpen stalwarts Alex Vesia and Evan Phillips and Skubal. Four others – Freeman, outfielder Teoscar Hernandez, third baseman Max Muncy and utility player Hyeseong Kim – are entering the final year of their contracts in 2027, though all but Freeman have club options for 2028.
If the Dodgers are going to change things by their own hand (as opposed to CBA mandate), Teoscar Hernandez clearly has a target on his back as the most likely Dodger to be traded this winter, clearing left field for De Paula. But the Dodgers have largely painted themselves into a corner with this roster. Freeman, shortstop Mookie Betts, catcher Will Smith, center fielder Andy Pages, right fielder Kyle Tucker, two-way star Shohei Ohtani and Muncy, each a year older, are all likely to be in the starting lineup on Opening Day 2027 – whenever that might be.
“I have no idea,” Muncy said of the potential for changes before next season. “That’s for people above me to make those decisions and it’s for me to show up next year, ready to go with whatever group we’ve got. There will come a time when we think about next year. But that’s not at this moment.”
Showing up at Camelback Ranch next spring with the same core is not necessarily a bad thing. Even with only minimal changes, the Dodgers will enter 2027 as the favorites in the National League West once again and a 15th consecutive postseason berth would bring another chance to win the “crapshoot” October has become.
But it also brings this Dodger core closer to “the cliff” Friedman has talked about avoiding.
“It’s tricky because you have to find the right balance,” he said. “It’s hard to transition young players onto your roster. It’s a hard adjustment from Triple-A to the major-league level. We’ve done it some over the years. Some guys we haven’t had the patience long enough to kind of see it through (perhaps an allusion to infielder Miguel Vargas, now an All-Star for the Chicago White Sox).
“That’s the challenge we have with the expectations we have. So we have to be mindful of having a really high standard but also transitioning some of our young players. We’ve seen it some, Andy Pages is featured prominently for us, Will Smith, Alex Freeland got a lot of opportunities this year. Dalton Rushing was a big part when Will missed time. And then late in the year we saw with Josue De Paula.
“We’ve got a lot of guys coming after that as well. So for us it’s about almost having a split personality – to do everything we can to maximize our chances of winning with our major-league roster, and the other side of our personality is pouring ourselves into doing everything we can to have as much talent coming, and we feel really good about that part as well.”

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — After their earliest postseason exit in three years, the Los Angeles Dodgers head into the offseason facing uncertainty over next year.
Shohei Ohtani was dogged by injuries to his left knee and right biceps over the second half and into the playoffs that rendered him ineffective at the plate. The two-way superstar also didn't pitch after the All-Star break.
Whether Ohtani needs offseason surgery remains to be seen, although he acknowledged it's possible after Thursday's loss to the Brewers that completed Milwaukee's sweep of the NL Championship Series. If he does, would the recovery bleed into the start of next season?
A potential MLB lockout is looming with the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1. Team owners have proposed a salary cap — something the sport has never had — and the players' union has adamantly rejected the idea.
A work stoppage would give Ohtani extra time to heal, although during such time the Dodgers would be cut off from communicating with any player, leaving Ohtani to rehab either from possible surgery or from his injuries on his own.
Communication between Ohtani and the team on his health during the season was “awesome,” Andrew Friedman, president of baseball operations, said last month, but he added: “The fully sharing exactly how he's feeling, maybe not so awesome.”
Ohtani said he plans to resume pitching next year, when he'll turn 33 in July. He's already had two Tommy John surgeries.
“What he’s doing is unprecedented, and it takes a real toll,” Friedman said. “And as you get older, I think us just being very dialed is going to be really important.”
Roster turnover is likely, even without big changes in MLB spending rules
The Dodgers had baseball's second-highest opening day payroll this year at $323.3 million, behind the New York Mets at $358.4 million. If a salary cap were to be imposed, the Dodgers' spending would be constrained when play resumes.
Some of the roster could look different next year, too, with nine players set to become free agents after the World Series, led by two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, who is expected to command a huge deal.
The Dodgers acquired Skubal from Detroit just before the trade deadline in August. The left-hander was 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 10 regular-season games for his new team. In the postseason, he was 1-1 with a 2.45 ERA and 14 Ks. Skubal didn't want to discuss his future Thursday, although he expressed enthusiasm for the organization, his teammates and the fans.
Advertisement
Other impending free agents are infielder Miguel Rojas, utility player Kiké Hernández, and relievers Kris Bubic, Brusdar Graterol, Eric Lauer, Evan Phillips, Blake Treinen and Alex Vesia.
As expected, Rojas announced his retirement Thursday, saying, “This is it, guys. That was my last game played.” He'll still be around, though, to work in a player development role.
Dodgers add a bit of youth with De Paula
The Dodgers got a glimpse of the future when they promoted Josue De Paula directly from Double-A to the majors in September. His energy and at-bats at designated hitter during Ohtani's stint on the injured list made an impression, and the 21-year-old was added to the postseason roster as a pinch-hitter.
The team will look to De Paula to further improve as an outfielder in 2027, although finding playing time for him will be challenging given the trio of veteran starters: Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker. De Paula is also blocked at DH by Ohtani.
“I think the experience he got being up here and watching what our guys do on a daily basis just helped connect some dots for him,” Friedman said. “And so, physically, he is capable of being a good corner outfielder, and we’re going to continue to tap into that.”
Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Ohtani, Tucker, Max Muncy and Will Smith will remain the Dodgers' veteran core. But some supporting players could be offloaded, like Kiké Hernández. Playing on a one-year deal, the 35-year-old was limited to 41 games while recovering from injuries and he didn't provide his usual postseason pop.
Manager Dave Roberts refused to blame an aging lineup for getting swept by the Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were three more than the Dodgers.
“We got beat,” he said. “There’s no because we’re too old or whatever. Every facet of the game, if you kind of unpack it, we were bested.”
There's drama off the field, too.
Owner Mark Walter was noticeably absent from the team's playoff games. He is facing multiple federal investigations into his business empire for possible financial improprieties involving insurance companies he controls. Walter has denied any wrongdoing. Since August, he sold his controlling interest in the Los Angeles Lakers and last month he unloaded his share in Chelsea of the Premier League.
___

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] As Dodgers grapple with the end of a dynasty, questions abound for Shohei Ohtani, free agency and the coming labor fight
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz
item.description: LOS ANGELES — In the end, the unfamiliarity outshined the shock. The defeated 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers, many of them back-to-back champs, hadn't been forced to face this uncomfortable silence in a while. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — In the end, the unfamiliarity outshined the shock.
The defeated 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers, many of them back-to-back champs, hadn't been forced to face this uncomfortable silence in a while. A four-game drubbing courtesy of the Milwaukee Brewers in a stunningly comprehensive NLCS sweep cast onto the most expensive team ever assembled a very foreign feeling: failure.
Milwaukee, so often bounced early in the October melee, knows that discomfort and its soundtrack. That unsettling hush that comes with the humbling unmooring of a premature postseason exit. Hugs, daps, thank yous, low-volume answers, goodbyes, regrets. But here it was, here the Dodgers were, in the tricked-out home clubhouse grappling with the end of something.
On one side of the room, Shohei Ohtani stood in front of his locker before a massive semicircle of reporters and TV cameras. For the first time in his MLB career, he'd lost a postseason series. His signing with L.A. ahead of the 2024 season sparked this era of supercharged dominance. And for eight October series his Dodgers were untouchable. Usually, during this spot in the calendar, Ohtani is getting drenched in imitation champagne as Latin rap and joyous roars echo in the background.
The scene Thursday night was a drier, quieter experience.
Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season
This seemingly indomitable baseball behemoth donned street clothes and a New Balance backward cap, small beads of sweat still pooling on his face, trying to explain what went wrong and where he goes from here.
"I haven't been able to really come to grips in terms of what I've learned overall this season," Ohtani said via interpreter Will Ireton. "I'm going to go back to the drawing board in terms of treatment, training program and see what I can come up with next season."
The postmortem on Los Angeles' crash-out can be as extensive as you choose to make it. But simply put, they were the inferior team. Slower, older, colder and less fearsome than the hard-charging Brewers. Baseball's most aged offense failed to slug and didn't perform with runners in scoring position. One of the most talented rotations ever assembled wasn't dominant enough to make up the difference.
All season, the Dodgers touted their experience as a calling card. Perhaps, if the series had been closer, that might have mattered. As it stands, it's less necessary to assign blame when so much went wrong.
"I think for me, it never feels good to lose, but when you get beat, you can handle it a little bit better," manager Dave Roberts said after his team's 6-4 loss in Game 4.
The morning after, fans across the baseball universe are celebrating the Dodgers' downfall. They aren't the only ones. As Milwaukee's champagne celebration roared in the visiting clubhouse, Brewers coaches and executives were already receiving texts of appreciation and congratulations on slaying the mighty dragon.
But don't expect the upcoming small-market Fall Classic to remedy baseball's impending labor struggle. With the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1, the league and the owners have been pushing hard for the adoption of a salary cap. Certainly, that argument becomes at least somewhat trickier to make with the half-billion-dollar boogeyman Dodgers on vacation, but the league won't suddenly change course after four games. The showdown over a cap was always going to be drawn-out and messy, no matter which team is the last one standing.
For the Dodgers organization, the uncertainty about baseball's future further complicates what was always going to be a critical offseason. One October exit won't kill off this juggernaut. Neither will a new economic landscape. The Dodgers remain advantageously positioned to compete for championships over the next decade and beyond. That's a testament to both their player-development prowess and their imposing spending power.
But the questions are already piling on Andrew Friedman's desk. Surely, the president of baseball operations is already considering the future and how this winter will shape the 2027 Dodgers.
No task is more important than figuring out what went wrong with Ohtani's season. For three months, the two-way star was, for the first time as a Dodger, doing full two-way stardom. Another MVP felt like an inevitability. Then his biceps started barking. A start on the mound was pushed back, then scratched, then so was another. Ohtani didn't throw a single in-game pitch after July 3.
His attempts to get back on the mound then appeared to compromise his offensive talents. He got ice-cold in late August into September. His physicality began to fray. His body wasn't right. Eventually, the Dodgers had no choice but to place him on the injured list. Only over the last two days of the Dodgers' postseason did Ohtani look anything like himself.
Communication with the four-time MVP has rarely been perfect. Some of that is the language barrier. Some of that is Ohtani's lone ranger approach. But now both sides need to evaluate why a diminished version of Ohtani was forced to play through pain. After the Game 4 loss, Ohtani told reporters that he intends to pitch next season. In what capacity remains to be seen. It might behoove the Dodgers to slow-play his recovery timeline to ensure he's available when they need him most — in the postseason.
There are a mountain of transactional questions as well. Tarik Skubal, added in a deadline blockbuster, is now a free agent. Will the Dodgers flex their muscles to re-sign him? Or do they want to give younger arms such as Roki Sasaki, Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski some rotation runway? What about upper-level pitching prospects such as Christian Zazueta, Zach Root, Adam Serwinowski and Jackson Ferris? Could they let Skubal walk in favor of a different free-agent starter? Freddy Peralta has looked pretty good recently.
Positionally, though, is where Los Angeles' bigger roster-construction conversations will take place. They got mollywhopped by Milwaukee in part because the Dodgers' offense looked unathletic and elderly. Friedman has expressed a desire to inject more youth into the group, but that's easier said than done. A number of spots feel set in stone: Ohtani at DH, Will Smith at catcher, Freddie Freeman at first, Mookie Betts at short, Kyle Tucker in right field, Andy Pages in center.
Max Muncy (3B) and Teoscar Hernández (LF) are older players expected to reach free agency after 2027. A trade of either could be a way to reshuffle the deck, with Hernández the likelier to go. Tommy Edman had a second straight mediocre, injury-marred campaign, but he has four seasons left on his contract. Might the Dodgers seek a suitor for the switch-hitting utilityman?
Even after harvesting the farm for the Skubal trade, Los Angeles has one of the most stocked systems in the sport. Most of their prospect juice is concentrated in the outfield. Five Dodgers outfield prospects at Double-A or above — Josue De Paula, Eduardo Quintero, Mike Sirota, Charles Davalan and James Tibbs III — could find themselves on offseason top-100 lists. De Paula, who impressed in a late-season cup of coffee, Quintero and Sirota are currently ranked fourth, 15th and 17th, respectively, by MLB Pipeline.
Unfortunately for the Dodgers, you can play only three outfielders at a time. In their existing outfield, they already have the highest-paid player in the sport (Tucker) and the starting center fielder in the 2026 All-Star Game (Pages). With just one spot remaining, it'll be fascinating to see how Friedman makes use of his farm system.
For the players, none of these contingencies or scenarios will offer any short-term solace. They aimed for a three-peat and missed. That sting will take time to subside, even if the 2027 Dodgers project to be a similarly formidable force.
"We fell short, you know?" utilityman Kiké Hernández lamented postgame. "We had a good run, but here we are."

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Max Muncy Reflects on the Last 3 Seasons of Dodger Baseball
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — Max Muncy had grown used to October ending with a celebration. Standing in the Dodgers’ clubhouse after Milwaukee completed its NLCS sweep, he was reminded how much the other ending hurts. “We haven’t had to do this in several years, and so you almost kind of forget how bad this sucks,” Muncy said. “It just meant so much to us, and we fell short.” “On that note, congratulations to the Brewers. They played really, really well,” he said. “They’re going to be a tough team in the W
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Max Muncy had grown used to October ending with a celebration. Standing in the Dodgers’ clubhouse after Milwaukee completed its NLCS sweep, he was reminded how much the other ending hurts.
“We haven’t had to do this in several years, and so you almost kind of forget how bad this sucks,” Muncy said. “It just meant so much to us, and we fell short.”
“On that note, congratulations to the Brewers. They played really, really well,” he said. “They’re going to be a tough team in the World Series.”
“We Left It All Out There”
The Dodgers’ bid for a third straight championship ended with a four-game sweep and another lead they couldn’t hold. Muncy acknowledged how poorly the team had played while reflecting on everything the group had poured into the past three years.
“It’s a special group, special clubhouse,” he said. “It’s kind of hard to put into words how much this hurts right now.”
“We all know what we did out there. We didn’t play well. But for three years straight, we left it all out there, and the train finally ran out of steam, I guess. But yeah, this just sucks.”
Asked about the brotherhood within the team, Muncy spoke warmly about the players sharing that disappointment.
“Absolutely. This clubhouse is special, and the guys that we have in here, it’s really special… I wouldn’t want to go through this with any other group of guys.”
“We’ve really, really created something special in this clubhouse. And I know next year we’re going to be ready to get right back to it. But for right now, this sucks.”
Gratitude Through the Heartbreak
The first moments after the loss brought the hurt everyone would expect. Muncy also saw room for gratitude toward teammates who had kept working through a long season.
“Everyone’s obviously very disappointed,” he said. “But we went through so much that, once you get over the heartbreak of it, I feel like there’s just a feeling of gratitude for the amount of work that every single guy in this clubhouse put in.”
“None of us quit, and we went out there and we tried to play as hard as we could, and ultimately we got beat.”
The Chances They Couldn’t Cash In
The Dodgers had chances to change Thursday’s outcome, stranding runners in scoring position in each of the sixth, seventh and eighth innings. Muncy gave Milwaukee’s bullpen credit while owning his team’s failure to deliver.
“I think it’s a little bit of both,” he said. “I think it’s their bullpen being extremely good and making pitches, and then I think it’s us just not getting the job done.”
“Ultimately, that’s why this damn thing is so hard. Just getting to the end is really, really, really hard.”
After two straight titles, the Dodgers had hoped to finish the climb once more. Muncy knew how many things had to come together to make that happen.
“I don’t know if people talk about it enough, but you have to have a lot of things go your way,” he said. “You have to have a little luck.; you have to have skill. Of course, you have to have talent. You have to have decisions, and it all has to kind of go your way to get to the end.”
“And we didn’t have it this year.”
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ÁNGELES – Los Dodgers se preparan para un largo invierno. Por primera vez en tres años, el equipo se va a casa sin el trofeo en sus manos, después de quedarse cortos en su intento de conseguir el tricampeonato al ser barridos en cuatro juegos por los Cerveceros en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional.
Sin embargo, ahora se abre una caja de Pandora para el club.
Desde hace un tiempo, los Dodgers mostraban algunas fallas estructurales que simplemente estaban siendo tapadas por los triunfos. No es para menos, pero cuando se acaban las victorias, esas carencias parecen exponenciarse.
A continuación, cuatro factores que deben monitorear los Dodgers para intentar sostener la dinastía que les ha visto ganar tres títulos en seis temporadas.
Veteranía
Este era el secreto a voces más popular de las Mayores. Los Dodgers son el equipo de mayor edad colectiva en MLB. Vaya, no por nada el dominicano Teóscar Hernández gritó: “¡Somos dinosaurios!” cuando destapaban el champán en esta postemporada.
Hasta entonces era un chiste, pero ahora debe ser tomado en cuenta con seriedad.
Freddie Freeman (37), Max Muncy (36), Mookie Betts (34), Teóscar Hernández (34), Enrique "Kiké" Hernández (35), Blake Snell (33) y Tyler Glasnow (33), entre otros, conforman un grupo de veteranos de mil batallas, que inició la temporada con un promedio de edad de 30.6 años, el más alto en las Grandes Ligas.
Y aunque en su mayoría siguen rindiendo, la edad es un factor invencible, ya sea con la debacle en los números o con la continua ausencia por lesiones.
De hecho, uno que sí ha bajado su producción consistentemente en los últimos dos años es el corazón de este grupo; Mookie Betts, quien viene de batear .257/.326/.454, segundo año seguido con OPS bajo .790 contra .874 de por vida, y en la postemporada cero empujadas en ocho juegos.
Por su parte, Freeman: OPS+ de 118 contra 140 de por vida, y de 14-1 en la serie.
Lesiones
Este factor ya ha empezado a pesar.
Entre todos los jugadores y a lo largo de 34 pasantías por la lista de lesionados, se acumularon 2,318 días perdidos en combinado. Parece un número inventado, pero no lo es. Sólo el hecho de ser el caso, ya prende las alarmas.
Fue la segunda cifra más alta en las Mayores, lo que curiosamente representa una ligera mejoría. Encabezaron la liga en días de ausencia por lesión en las tres temporadas previas.
Hay años en los que reina la mala suerte con la salud, y puede que ese sea el caso. Pero, cuando se toma en cuenta la edad, no se puede ignorar esta realidad.
Contratos
Con la ventana de competencia abierta, los Dodgers hicieron lo necesario para continuar compitiendo, siendo bien creativos con la estructuración de los contratos ofrecidos.
Pero en medio de un mar de acuerdos, hay algunos que también disparan la atención, especialmente los más recientes.
Kyle Tucker fue el mejor jugador de los Dodgers en la SCLN y posiblemente de los playoffs, pero eso no erradica del todo la deficiente temporada regular que tuvo, registrando .233/.330/.385, 17 jonrones y 70 empujadas en 154 juegos.
Su contrato es de US$240 millones por cuatro años, y aunque tiene cláusulas de salida, de no mejorar su producción, es probable que no sean activadas.
Después está el pacto con el puertorriqueño Edwin Díaz, de tres años y US$69 millones. Terminó con EFE de 8.68 y 7 salvados en 11 oportunidades, con cirugía de codo en abril y otro pase por la IL. Se redimió con dos salvados en la SDLN, pero en los primeros tres juegos de esta serie no lanzó ni un solo pitcheo, porque los Dodgers nunca tuvieron ventaja tarde.
Hay otros casos a revisar en la nómina, pero ciertamente estos dos son dignos de resaltar.
Ohtani
Este es el factor principal, sin duda.
Ser un jugador de dos vías es lo que Ohtani ejemplifica. Es quien es. Sin embargo, en tres años con los Dodgers no ha podido cumplir ambas funciones durante una temporada entera. Después de estar apartado completamente del montículo durante el primer año en Los Ángeles, después estuvo tiempo rehabilitándose en el 2025. Este parecía ser el año, pero a mediados de temporada, el cuerpo le comenzó a pasar factura, hasta que eventualmente se decidió que no volvería a lanzar. El problema es que no volvió a ser el mismo al bate tampoco.
Cuando estuvo en doble función, rindió no sólo a nivel de Jugador Más Valioso, sino de Cy Young. Sobre la loma, registró récord de 8-2 y efectividad de 1.79. Pero entonces aparecieron los problemas físicos, y desde que se vio obligado a apartarse del montículo, su ofensiva también decayó. Desde el 3 de julio, bateó .257/.336/.495 con OPS de .831, 12 jonrones y 31 empujadas en 54 encuentros. No son números malos, pero no son de Ohtani.
De nuevo, es difícil que Ohtani deje de ser un jugador multifacético, pero ciertamente es un factor que determinará el éxito de los Dodgers en los próximos años.

item.title: [CBS Sports] What's next for the Dodgers? Futures of Shohei Ohtani, Tarik Skubal uncertain after elimination

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers dynasty is over, or has at least hit a major bump in the road. Thursday's Game 4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers completed the four-game sweep and sent the two-time defending World Series champions home for the winter. Los Angeles' season is over, as is its stretch of eight consecutive postseason series wins dating back to 2024.
There is no getting around it: The Dodgers looked old in the NLCS. They are old too. Weighed by playing time, they had baseball's oldest collection of position players this season. Will Smith is 31. Shohei Ohtani is 32. Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernández are 34. Freddie Freeman is 37. The team's core hitters are getting long in the tooth. It was obvious in the NLCS.
That said, the Dodgers remain extremely talented and have the resources (money and tradeable prospects) to improve their roster in the offseason, and again contend in 2027. As bad as they looked in the NLCS, there is no reason to think the Dodgers won't be among baseball's best teams next year -- and on the short list of legitimate World Series contenders.
Here now are three questions facing the Dodgers following their unceremonious NLCS sweep.
1. What is Shohei Ohtani's future?
The two-way star was hindered by health for a large chunk of 2026
In fact, let's talk about his future both short- and long-term. Ohtani was clearly diminished late in the regular season and into the postseason. He played through knee and biceps injuries and simply did not look like himself at the plate. His swing was all arms and there was little hard contact. Before his second-inning home run in Game 4 on Thursday, Ohtani hadn't gone deep since Aug. 18. His power vanished.
Here is Ohtani's expected slugging percentage, which is based on contact quality (exit velocity, launch angle, etc.), throughout this season. It slipped significantly late in the year:
Ohtani did not pitch after July 3 and had a start-and-stop in late August. He rehabbed his injuries, threw bullpen sessions and live batting practice, then had to shut it down before getting back on a mound in a game. Ohtani was playing like his usual MVP self until his injuries popped up in the second half. Once that happened, his season began to circle the drain.
The Dodgers now face two questions with Ohtani. One, does he need offseason surgery on the knee and/or biceps? And if he does need surgery, will the recovery cut into his 2027? Keep in mind that it is a near certainty there will be a lockout this offseason once the CBA expires on Dec. 1, and teams will be banned from communicating with their players. Ohtani would have to rehab on his own, without the team's input.
"It's hard to tell" if he'll require surgery, Ohtani said through an interpreter after Thursday's loss. He does, however, plan to pitch next season, he said.
Offseason surgery is the short-term question. Long-term, regardless of what he said in the shadow of the NLCS sweep, are Ohtani's days as a pitcher numbered? This has been a question since Day 1 of Ohtani's MLB career. His ability to be and remain a two-way player has long been doubted, but he has kept doing it, even if there have been some speed bumps along the way. Ohtani has made a career of doing what people said he couldn't.
The man is 32 now, though. He'll turn 33 next summer and the physical ailments (the knee, the biceps, two UCL surgeries, etc.) are beginning to add up. At some point, Ohtani won't be able to continue as a two-way player, and with each passing season, that point draws closer. Are we there now? Is this it? Is this the end of Ohtani's time as a pitcher? It could be, sure.
My guess is that Ohtani will continue to pitch next season and the Dodgers will happily let him because there is so much value to be gained even if he throws only 75 innings a year. You can't be as good as Ohtani without being stubborn. He's been stubborn in that he insists on playing both ways, and he has continued to do it well. I don't see him dropping it this winter.
It should surprise no one if Ohtani comes out next year, hits 40 home runs, makes 15 ace-caliber starts and wins his fifth MVP unanimously. Do not forget that he was playing at that level as recently as July. The recovery times for the knee and biceps injuries are an offseason question, for sure, and the bottom line is the "will he continue to pitch?" questions will always exist.
2. Will they move on from some longtime stalwarts?
Could the Dodgers say goodbye to Teoscar Hernández or some other familiar names?
The Dodgers are locked into so much of their core: Betts, Freeman, Ohtani, Smith, Kyle Tucker, etc. They aren't going anywhere. That said, there are a few members of the supporting cast, players who have been around for all three recent World Series wins, who might have to be shown the door this offseason for the sake of diversifying the lineup and getting younger and more athletic.
Finding a taker for the final season of Teoscar Hernández's contract and then plugging the precocious Josue De Paula into left field next season is a worthwhile move. It's difficult because Hernández is popular in the clubhouse, but, on the field, De Paula figures to give the Dodgers a better chance to win ballgames moving forward. (De Paula is a poor defender, but so is Hernández.)
The Enrique Hernández era has run its course. He hasn't been even an average regular-season player since 2022, and, for all his postseason heroics, he's barely scraping a .600 OPS in the last two Octobers. Tommy Edman is a better version of the same player. There's no need to carry both on the roster, plus Edman's injuries suggest a smaller role is needed. Less could be more.
Max Muncy stayed healthy this season, hit 29 homers and posted 4.1 WAR, and is owed an affordable $10 million in 2027. Plus, it's a bad offseason to need an infielder. The free-agent market is very thin and you're not likely to find better than Muncy on the trade market. Still, he is 36. Keeping Muncy is justifiable, but it also makes sense to explore alternatives. It never hurts to look.
Blake Treinen has not been healthy and effective at the same time in two years. Alex Vesia's fastball sat 91-92 mph over these last few weeks. Both are free agents and the Dodgers have so many young hard-throwers in Triple-A that I think it's worth turning the page and injecting some younger arms into the bullpen. Evan Phillips may be in this camp, too.
Then again, who am I to doubt the Dodgers and their process? Disappointing NLCS aside, they have been baseball's most successful team of the 2020s, and if they want to remain in the Hernández and Muncy and Treinen business, I won't say they're wrong. It does appear that things are getting a bit stale, though. Incorporating youth would be sensible, and it isn't difficult to find ways to do it.
3. Will they retain Tarik Skubal?
It will cost a lot to keep the trade deadline addition atop the rotation
There's no sense in asking if the Dodgers can retain Tarik Skubal. Of course they can. They are baseball's biggest spenders and he is a Scott Boras client. Typically, all you need to do to get a Boras client is make the biggest offer, which the Dodgers can do. Maybe there's a salary cap that changes the equation. Based on what we know right now, yes, the Dodgers can, of course, re-sign Skubal.
Will they is a different matter. Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, and Yoshinobu Yamamoto will return next season. Ohtani could be back on the mound as well, as he indicated is the plan. Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski both pitched well for long stretches this year and are among the very best No. 5 starter options in the game. Gavin Stone, the team's 2024 innings leader, should return from shoulder surgery as well.
There is never a bad time to sign a pitcher like Skubal, and the Dodgers, with their World Series window still open, are well-positioned to bring him back. They have the money, they can easily clear rotation space, and all indications are that Skubal enjoyed his time with the team after coming over the trade deadline. This feels like a match made in free-agent heaven.
Now it's just a matter of whether the Dodgers can get it done. Perhaps a salary cap or increased competitive balance tax penalties limit their spending; maybe they opt to spread their money around to multiple players; maybe another team just won't be denied. The Dodgers don't absolutely need Skubal. Re-signing him would up their odds of returning to the World Series, though, and help ensure their dynasty didn't end on Thursday night.
For his part, Skubal declined to comment on his impending decision after Game 4.
"I'm not going to comment on my future really at all," Skubal said, via MLB.com. "Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at."

item.title: [Orange County Register] Dodgers waste late opportunities as failures in the clutch burn them again in NLCS finale
item.dc:creator: Jeff Fletcher
item.description: LOS ANGELES — With all their financial might, the Dodgers couldn’t buy a hit when they needed it most. The Dodgers’ bid for a three-peat came to an end, in large part because their star-studded lineup managed just four hits in 27 at-bats with runners in scoring position while losing all four games of the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — With all their financial might, the Dodgers couldn’t buy a hit when they needed it most.
The Dodgers’ bid for a three-peat came to an end, in large part because their star-studded lineup managed just four hits in 27 at-bats with runners in scoring position while losing all four games of the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers.
Was it the excellence of the Brewers’ pitchers or the failure of the Dodgers’ hitters in those moments?
“It’s a little bit of both,” Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy said. “I think it’s their bullpen being extremely good and making pitches, and then I think it’s us just not getting the job done, but ultimately, that’s why this damn thing is so hard, you know? Just getting to the end is just really, really, really hard. I don’t know if people talk about it enough, but you have to have a lot of things go your way. You have to have a little luck. You have to have skill. You have to have talent. You have to have decisions, and it all has to kind of go your way to get to the end and we just didn’t have it this year.”
There were signs in the second half of the season that the Dodgers weren’t firing on all cylinders, when their offense began to slow down. And even in winning their NL Division Series against the Atlanta Braves, their power covered up the problem.
The Dodgers managed to hit eight homers in that series, accounting for 11 of their 14 runs.
They were 1 for 16 with runners in scoring position. For the postseason, they were 5 for 43.
Two of those hits came in the second inning on Thursday, when Andy Pages punched a run-scoring single up the middle and then Shohei Ohtani hit a three-run homer.
At that point, the Dodgers had a 4-0 lead and the ballpark was rocking. The party seemed like it was just starting, but it was actually ending.
The Dodgers didn’t get another hit with a runner in scoring position in the game.
“I don’t know,” outfielder Teoscar Hernandez said. “I think better decisions when it comes to swinging the bat. But sometimes you’ve got to give the other side credit, you know? They have one of the best bullpens in the history of baseball. It’s hard when you’re facing a guy that is attacking you with everything that they got and and making pitches, being aggressive and you don’t get the results that you want.”
The final four innings of Game 4 were particularly painful for the Dodgers. Just after the Brewers took a 5-4 lead in the top of the sixth, the Dodgers had a runner in scoring position in three straight innings.
The Dodgers went hitless in six official at-bats with runners in scoring position – plus one sacrifice. In two of those, they had a runner at third with less than two outs.
The frustrating sequence began when Kyle Tucker ripped a one-out double in the sixth, but Hernandez grounded out and Muncy struck out.
In the seventh, Pages led off with a double. After Kiké Hernandez bunted him to third, Ohtani struck out on three pitches and then Mookie Betts grounded out.
With one out in the eighth, Will Smith ripped one down the right field line, for a double, and he took third base as the ball skipped past right fielder Sal Frelick.
Just 90 feet from a tie game, the Dodgers came up empty again. Tucker hit a fly ball to shallow center field and then Hernandez struck out.
The Dodgers went down in order in the ninth, ending their season.
Afterward, first baseman Freddie Freeman was asked how “deflating” it was to continually come up empty in so many opportunities when they just needed a hit.
“Everything’s deflating now,” Freeman said. “I know there wasn’t one pitch, one at-bat. They just outplayed us in the series, which is kind of how it goes. We had our opportunities. We didn’t get the job done.”

item.title: [dailyadvance.com] Brewers sweep the Dodgers in the NLCS to reach the World Series for the first time since 1982
item.dc:creator: BETH HARRIS
item.description: LOS ANGELES (AP) — Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer in the sixth inning, Milwaukee's brilliant bullpen slammed the door late and the Brewers rallied past the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4 on Thursday in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series to earn their first World Series trip since 1982. No. 9 hitter David Hamilton's two-out solo shot off Edwin Díaz gave the Brewers a two-run cushion in the ninth. Hamilton had just four homers in the regular season. “We got down early tonight and we
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Garrett Mitchell hit a go-ahead homer in the sixth inning, Milwaukee's brilliant bullpen slammed the door late and the Brewers rallied past the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4 on Thursday in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series to earn their first World Series trip since 1982.
No. 9 hitter David Hamilton's two-out solo shot off Edwin Díaz gave the Brewers a two-run cushion in the ninth. Hamilton had just four homers in the regular season.
“We got down early tonight and we were like, it’s going to be a great story,” Brewers captain Christian Yelich said. “We’re going to come back and win this. Like, stay together, start chipping away. And that’s exactly what they did.”
Aaron Ashby pitched three scoreless innings for a save as the Brewers erased a four-run deficit to win their first NL pennant and second overall. Milwaukee was in the American League when the franchise made its only previous World Series appearance 44 years ago, a seven-game loss to the St. Louis Cardinals.
Shohei Ohtani's first home run this postseason helped put the Dodgers ahead 4-0 in the second inning before the Brewers came back to complete a four-game sweep of the two-time defending World Series champions a year after getting swept by Los Angeles in the NLCS.
“They may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we’ve got a bunch of gamers — and the gamers won this week,” Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said.
The Dodgers' goal of a three-peat — not done since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 and never by a National League team — died with their anemic offense and injuries to Ohtani and others on their aging roster.
“I'm not used to those consolation speeches,” manager Dave Roberts said. “The thing about sports that we all love is no matter how much you prepare, you want it, there’s no guarantees.”
After topping the majors with 103 wins during the regular season, Milwaukee became the first major league club to finish a postseason sweep after getting swept by that same opponent in the previous postseason.
The Brewers also are the first team to sweep a best-of-seven postseason series in which it trailed in every game.
“There was never a doubt in that dugout what was going to happen tonight. We knew we were going to win that game,” said first baseman Jake Bauers, the NLCS MVP.
With the score tied 4-all, Mitchell fell behind 0-2 before reliever Tanner Scott threw three straight balls for a full count. Mitchell’s 409-foot leadoff drive to center field — the first homer of his career on an 0-2 count — put the Brewers ahead for the first time. Mitchell also homered in their 6-2 victory Wednesday.
“It’s absolutely surreal," Mitchell said. "You talk about the battle-tested Brewers. We went down early and the belief in that dugout got stronger and stronger.”
The Brewers’ bullpen coolly turned away multiple threats when the Dodgers had the potential tying run on base.
Winning pitcher JoJo Romero struck out Max Muncy with Kyle Tucker at third to end the sixth.
With one out in the seventh and a runner on third, Ashby struck out Ohtani swinging before Mookie Betts grounded out to end the inning. Will Smith doubled to right with one out in the eighth and was safe at third when the ball got away from Sal Frelick for an error before Ashby got Tucker to fly out and Teoscar Hernández to strike out.
“Playing with that chip on our shoulder,” Ashby said. “You don’t ever know what to expect going into a series like that last year (against the Dodgers). You don’t know how bad it can be, and then it was as bad as it was. And we came out and we survived, and we came back this year, and those guys played their tails off.”
The Brewers tied it in the fifth, when the Dodgers bullpen issued four walks and Milwaukee stole two bases. Hamilton’s single chased starter Tyler Glasnow and scored Frelick, who walked and stole second, to pull Milwaukee to 4-3.
Alex Vesia came in and promptly walked Brice Turang and William Contreras to load the bases. Vesia then walked Bauers with two outs to force in Hamilton with the tying run.
Glasnow retired his first 10 batters — six on strikeouts — before the Brewers got to him in the fourth. Turang walked, Contreras hit a ground-rule double and Bauers followed with another ground-rule double that closed Milwaukee to 4-2.
Ohtani broke out of his postseason slump with a three-run homer after Andy Pages’ RBI single in the second. The four-time MVP released weeks of pent-up frustration by raising his arms and yelling and the crowd of 49,104 joined him in celebration.
But the Brewers wouldn't be denied. And when it was over, owner Mark Attanasio thought of Milwaukee's longtime owner and beloved late broadcaster.
“It’s so important for the community, the entire state of Wisconsin,” Attanasio said. “We’re standing on shoulders of Bud Selig and Bob Uecker.”

item.title: [sgvtribune.com] Dodgers’ Shohei Ohtani returns to leadoff spot for must-win Game 4
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett
item.description: LOS ANGELES — Desperate times call for … unexpected measures. Two days after admitting he had a conversation with Shohei Ohtani about taking him out of the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series and one day after dropping him to sixth in the order for that game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts moved Ohtani back to the top of the lineup. Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for Game 4 against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday. It was his first time batting leadoff this postseason. “J
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Desperate times call for … unexpected measures.
Two days after admitting he had a conversation with Shohei Ohtani about taking him out of the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series and one day after dropping him to sixth in the order for that game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts moved Ohtani back to the top of the lineup.
Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for Game 4 against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday. It was his first time batting leadoff this postseason.
“Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at,” Roberts said. “I liked the at-bats yesterday, and I felt that trying to shake it up a little bit – obviously we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to.”
Ohtani is just 4 for 22 (.182) in the postseason, but that hardly stands out in the unproductive lineup. Through the first three games of the NLCS, the Dodgers were hitting .165 (15 for 91) as a team with just two extra-base hits and no home runs. Only Mookie Betts (3 for 12) had more than two hits.
“I think getting back to what we’ve done all year and how it’s been going recently as far as on the offense, I think it warranted just a little bit of a shakeup,” said Roberts, who also started Miguel Rojas and Kiké Hernandez against Brewers left-hander Shane Drohan.
PHILLY CONNECTION
Before re-signing Don Mattingly to a contract extension as manager, the Philadelphia Phillies reached out to two members of the Dodgers’ front office with Philly connections – Chase Utley and Raul Ibañez.
Neither would confirm the contact, but neither interviewed for the job. Both have teen-aged children and Utley acknowledged family takes priority over pursuing a managerial career at this point.
Ibañez, currently the Dodgers’ vice president of baseball development and special projects, has been approached about managing on other occasions but declined. Utley is a special assistant to Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman.
AWARDS SEASON
Despite his injuries and a prolonged slump, Ohtani is one of the National League finalists for the Hank Aaron Award given to the top offensive performer in MLB during the regular season. Ohtani finished the season with a .275 average, 30 home runs and an .889 OPS. Ohtani has won it the past three seasons (twice in the NL and once with the Angels in the American League).
The other finalists are CJ Abrams (Washington Nationals), Jake Bauers (Milwaukee Brewers), Pete Crow-Armstrong (Chicago Cubs), Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart (Cincinnati Reds), Matt Olson (Atlanta Braves), Kyle Schwarber (Philadelphia Phillies), Fernando Tatis Jr. (San Diego Padres) and Jordan Walker (St. Louis Cardinals).
Ohtani is also one of three finalists for the Players’ Choice Outstanding Player Award along with Crow-Armstrong and Schwarber.
Max Muncy and Andy Pages have been named finalists for Gold Glove awards at their positions. Muncy is a finalist at third base along with Alex Bregman (Cubs) and Javier Sanoja (Miami Marlins). Pages is a finalist in center field along with Crow-Armstrong and Michael Harris II (Braves).
The Gold Glove winners will be announced on ESPN on Nov. 1.
UP NEXT
NLCS Game 5 (if necessary): Brewers (RHP Jacob Misiorowski, 16-5, 1.80 ERA) at Dodgers (LHP Tarik Skubal, 12-7, 2.72 ERA), Friday, 6 p.m. FS1, 570 AM

item.title: [sgvtribune.com] Dodgers three-peat bid ends with NLCS sweep by Brewers
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett

His three-run home run in the second inning on Thursday night gave the Dodgers a four-run lead – unheard of in this postseason of run suppression.
