item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — In the end, it was all too much – coming back from a 3-0 deficit, winning a third consecutive World Series championship.
Shohei Ohtani came back to life after two months of ugly at-bats, unfamiliar criticism and questions about whether he even belonged in the Dodgers’ lineup. His three-run home run in the second inning on Thursday night gave the Dodgers a four-run lead – unheard of in this postseason of run suppression.
That wasn’t enough to keep their season alive against a relentless Milwaukee Brewers team that just kept coming, taking a 6-4 win in Game 4 on Thursday to complete a four-game sweep of the two-time defending champions and advance from the National League Championship Series to their first World Series in 44 years.
After falling behind on Garrett Mitchell’s home run off Tanner Scott in the sixth inning, the Dodgers put the tying run on third base with one out in the sixth, seventh and eighth innings but couldn’t move him another 90 feet. Their dreams of a three-peat were buried under another collection of failed at-bats with a runner in scoring position. They went 2 for 11 in those situations in Game 4 and 5 for 43 in the postseason.
“As a manager and anyone participating in the game, you always wonder … could we have done something different that could have changed the game?” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I think at the end of the day, we got beat. We got outplayed in all facets. Those guys played flawless defensively. They pitched better than we did. They hit better than we did. They slugged more than we did. You’ve got to sometimes just tip your cap.
“I personally told our guys that there’s no apologies, there’s no ‘Sorry’s. We gave it everything we had, and it wasn’t good enough. That’s part of life.”
The New York Yankees of 1998-2000 are still the most recent team to ‘three-peat’ as World Series champions. A National League franchise still hasn’t done it.
“It’s hard to win one. We won two,” Freddie Freeman said. “We went for three and we came up short on a third. Special stuff the past two years. We just came up short this year.”
After losing Game 3 on Wednesday night to become the 42nd team in MLB history to fall behind 3-0 in a best-of-seven series, the Dodgers said all the right things about becoming just the second to climb out of that hole and win the series.
“Four one-game winning streaks,” Dodgers utility player Kiké Hernandez said.
“We’ve won four in a row a number of times this year, ten times, I think,” Manager Dave Roberts said.
Ohtani gave them reason to believe.
With the Brewers rolling out a ‘bullpen game’ in Game 4, opener Shane Drohan was gone after a leadoff single by Kyle Tucker in the second inning. Former Dodger Dustin May replaced him and gave up another single to Teoscar Hernandez, struck out Max Muncy then gave up an RBI single to Andy Pages – the only Dodger who seemed able to hit with a runner in scoring position this postseason.
Kiké Hernandez flew out, bringing Ohtani to the plate with two outs. He struck out against Drohan in the first inning but had finished Game 3 with a 113.5 mph exit velocity on an eighth-inning single – the kind of hard contact missing from Ohtani since mid-August and one of the signs that convinced Roberts to move him back to the leadoff spot for Game 4.
May threw Ohtani a 1-and-1 cutter in at his knees and Ohtani crushed it. It left his bat at 113.1 mph and traveled 428 feet into the right field pavilion. The emotion that burst out of Ohtani was just as explosive. As the crowd roared, he bounced down the first-base line, screaming and gesturing at his teammates in the dugout.
It looked like things were finally turning the Dodgers’ way in this series.
“It’s hard to not say yeah to that,” Muncy said. “He gets that moment, it’s like that’s the swing we’ve been waiting for. We got a nice lead, we got Glas on the mound, we’re confident behind him and they just kept stringing together one good at-bat after another after another after another. They were just kind of relentless.”
The Dodgers’ first home run in the NLCS ended the longest home-run drought of Ohtani’s career at 25 games and 116 plate appearances.
The only thing that seemed longer was how long the Dodgers were going to have to work to make that four-run second inning stand up.
It began disappearing in the fourth inning.
Starter Tyler Glasnow retired the first 10 Brewers in order and struck out six of the first eight. He didn’t have another strikeout. It was nothing but contact from the Brewers after that.
A walk and back-to-back ground-rule doubles – the second by Jake Bauers – cut the Dodgers’ lead in half. An inning later, Glasnow walked the No. 8 hitter, Sal Frelick, who stole second and scored on a single by the No. 9 hitter David Hamilton.
Glasnow was replaced by Evan Phillips who walked three in a row (one intentionally after Hamilton stole second) to force in the tying run.
The four aces the Dodgers thought would give them the upper hand in this postseason did not. Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Glasnow combined for a 6.50 ERA in the series against the Brewers. Only Skubal allowed fewer than three runs in his start.
Tanner Scott came on for the sixth inning. He didn’t give up a home run to a left-handed batter all season. The Brewers’ first batter in the sixth, left-handed Garrett Mitchell, has just two home runs off left-handed pitchers in his 286 career regular-season games.
Scott left a full-count fastball over the heart of the plate and Mitchell, a former UCLA and Orange Lutheran standout, sent it over the center field wall for his second home run off a left-handed pitcher in three at-bats (Blake Snell in Game 3).
The Brewers’ bullpen took over from there. The Dodgers got Kyle Tucker to third base after his one-out double in the sixth, Pages to third after his leadoff double in the seventh and Will Smith to third when Brewers right fielder Frelick fumbled his double in the right field corner.
The six at-bats with a chance to push across the tying run ended in three strikeouts, two ground outs and a shallow pop up to center field.
Hamilton made it a two-run lead with a solo home run in the top of the ninth. It was just the fifth hit of the game for the Brewers.
More to come on this story.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Who's to blame for Dodgers' shocking NLCS loss vs. Brewers? Five places to point fingers
item.dc:creator: Mike Axisa
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers are going to the World Series for the second time in franchise history and the first time as a National League team (the Brewers were still in the American League when they went to the World Series in 1982). This also means the Los Angeles Dodgers have been eliminated, and their shot at becoming baseball's first threepeat champion since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees ended on Thursday night. The Brewers have swept the Dodgers in four games in the NLCS, doing so one year aft
item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers are going to the World Series for the second time in franchise history and the first time as a National League team (the Brewers were still in the American League when they went to the World Series in 1982). This also means the Los Angeles Dodgers have been eliminated, and their shot at becoming baseball's first threepeat champion since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees ended on Thursday night. The Brewers have swept the Dodgers in four games in the NLCS, doing so one year after the Dodgers swept them in the 2025 NLCS.
Who is to blame for the Dodgers going four-and-out in the NLCS? There's plenty of blame to go around, so let's assign it, shall we?
1. The Brewers
Milwaukee continues to be baseball's best team
We have to start here. The Dodgers got swept in the NLCS because the Brewers outplayed them in every phase of the game. The Brewers got better starting pitching. Their bullpen was better. Their defense and baserunning were better. Their offense was better at both stringing together hits to build a rally and launching the ball out of the park. Pat Murphy out-managed Dave Roberts as well. You name it, and the Brewers did it better than the Dodgers this series.
"It's a pretty simple answer," Dodgers infielder Max Muncy said after Game 3. "We're playing like shit. They're playing great."
As much as we want to (and will) blame various Dodgers for the sweep, the single biggest reason they got swept is that the Brewers were simply the better team. They were the better team in the regular season based on their records (103-59 vs. 100-62) and run differentials (+214 vs. +201), and they certainly played like the better team in the NLCS. The better team doesn't always win a postseason series. In the NLCS though, the better team has played like the better team, period.
2. Shohei Ohtani
MLB's brightest star was greatly dimmed ... even with Game 4 homer
The biggest star on baseball's most star-laden team was not himself the last two months of the season. Shohei Ohtani played through knee and biceps injuries and had been so unproductive than Roberts said there would at least be a "conversation" about sitting Ohtani in Game 3. That didn't come to pass, and hey, Ohtani went 1 for 2 with a walk and a hit-by-pitch in Game 3, and hit a home run in Game 4. The homer put the Dodgers up 4-0 on Thursday. The Dodgers didn't score again. The bottom line is Ohtani was a non-factor until it was too late. It's hard to win when your best player is this diminished.
Whenever a team loses in the postseason, the best player gets a disproportionate amount of the blame, and that applies to Ohtani this series. He's clearly not healthy, , and he's had multiple chances in the first three games to swing things in his team's favor, but couldn't do it. When the best player underperforms, he wears most of the blame. It has been the way of the world since the dawn of team sports.
3. Freddie Freeman
Normally clutch, Freeman has been the worst player in the series
Freddie Freeman, not Ohtani, was the worst player in the NLCS by both win probability added and championship probability added. He went 1 for 14 in the series and the one hit came in the first inning of Game 1. Freeman went 0 for 13 after his first NLCS at-bat and that 0 for 13 includes:
- Striking out after Mookie Betts worked a leadoff walk in the third inning of Game 1.
- Grounding into an inning-ending double play in the fifth inning of Game 1.
- Popping up to second on the first pitch to lead off the eighth inning of Game 1.
- Flying out with runners on first and second and no outs in the third inning of Game 2.
- Flying out with runners on first and second and one out in the third inning of Game 3.
- Grounding out with a runner on first and two outs in the fifth inning of Game 3.
That's an awful lot of empty at-bats in clutch situations for one of the best clutch hitters of this generation. Freeman had as many double plays as total bases (one each) in the NLCS, and his only RBI came on a sacrifice fly. You won't beat a team as good as the Brewers with sac flies. You need bigger swings from your best players and Freeman didn't provide them.
4. The supporting cast
Only two Dodgers hitters had consistently strong at-bats in the NLCS
Max Muncy went 2 for 12 with six strikeouts in the NLCS. Teoscar Hernández went 3 for 14. Andy Pages went 3 for 12. Tommy Edman went 1 for 7. Will Smith went 2 for 15 in the NLCS. Postseason legend Enrique Hernández went 0 for 8 with a ghasty strikeout in Game 3. The Dodgers had runners at second and third with one out in sixth, and Hernández took two pitches in the zone for strikes, then flailed at slider out of the zone. It was maybe the single worst at-bat of this NLCS.
Freeman was terrible, Ohtani was terrible, and the thing that has so often set the Dodgers apart these last few years -- an elite supporting cast -- was terrible as well. Edman, Muncy, Smith, and the Hernándezes are a combined 11 for 58 (.189) in the four games. Betts (3 for 15 with three walks) and Kyle Tucker (4 for 12 with three walks) were the only Dodgers hitters who escaped scrutiny. They were their most productive hitters and consistently had strong at-bats. Everyone else? 😴😴😴
5. Dave Roberts
Roberts did not push the right buttons
The manager can not swing the bat or throw the ball for his players, but he can put his team in the best position to succeed, and Roberts did not do that in the NLCS. Game 3, especially, was a managerial mess. Roberts burned the precocious Josue De Paula in the sixth inning when he sent him up to pinch-hit for Miguel Rojas with runners on second and third and one out, then immediately pinch-hit Enrique Hernández for De Paula when the Brewers brought in a lefty reliever.
De Paula is a rookie, I get that, but he has a track record of hitting lefties well in the minors. More accurately, he has a strong track record of making contact against lefties, which is what the Dodgers needed in that spot. A ball in play to get a run home. Instead, Roberts defaulted to the veteran Hernández, who struck out feebly. For all his career postseason success, Hernández went 1 for 14 this postseason, and a .190/.235/.317 hitter in his last 19 postseason games. Roberts never adjusted his priors.
The NLCS was a flashback to pre-2024 Roberts, when he too often showed too much faith in his veterans and had an unfortunate knack for sticking with starters too long. In 2024 and 2025, it all worked out, and Roberts looked like a genius. Those same mistakes, the ones he got away with the last two years, reared their ugly heads. The NLCS sweep is on the players, first and foremost. Roberts didn't play his cards well either. He's made things worse.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers face an offseason reckoning after stunning NLCS sweep
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: The home run shredded the October sky like a bolt of lightning. Shohei Ohtani turned toward the Dodgers’ bench. He threw his bat. He screamed. He punched the air. item.content:encoded:
The home run shredded the October sky like a bolt of lightning.
Shohei Ohtani turned toward the Dodgers’ bench.
He threw his bat. He screamed. He punched the air. He screamed some more.
With one furious swing, Ohtani unleashed months of pent-up frustration.
His streak of 115 plate appearances without a home run was over.
But this wasn’t a series-altering three-run home run.
This was a last stand.
The four-run lead the Dodgers built up in that stadium-rocking second inning didn’t endure. The Milwaukee Brewers saw that it wouldn’t.
As they did throughout this National League Championship Series, the Brewers pressed and pressed and pressed. Little by little, the Dodgers gave in.
By the sixth inning, the Dodgers were behind. Three innings later, they were officially eliminated from the playoffs when Kiké Hernández flied out to left field against Aaron Ashby for the final out of a 6-4 defeat at Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers didn’t just lose.
They were swept in four games by the same team they swept at this stage of the postseason last year.
Now, comes the hard part.
The Dodgers might be the second-best team in baseball behind the Brewers, but they can’t return with a similar roster next season and expect the results to be any different.
Farewells are in order.
Farewell to long-time Dodgers who will forever be known in these parts as World Series heroes.
Farewell to Ohtani hitting and pitching full-time.
With how the Dodgers were thumped by the Brewers, president of baseball operation Andrew Friedman has a clear directive.
Adjust – or else.
The Dodgers have the oldest team in the major leagues. First baseman Freddie Freeman and infielder Miguel Rojas are 37. Third baseman Max Muncy is 36 and utilityman Kiké Hernández is 35. Shortstop Mookie Betts and outfielder Teoscar Hernández are 34.
The problem is magnified by their prime-aged players, who are breaking down as if they are senior citizens.
Ohtani, 32, was obviously debilitated in the postseason, which explains why a former 50-homer player wasn’t a power threat for the majority of these playoffs.
Catcher Will Smith, 31, was sidelined for three months with a disc problem, which contributed to him being out of sorts in the batter’s box.
Utilityman Tommy Edman, also 31, is an All-Star-caliber player when healthy – but he often isn’t.
Kyle Tucker, 29, flat-out stunk for the majority of the first season of his four-year, $240-million contract.
What Friedman and others in the front office will have to decide in the coming weeks and months is how quickly and drastically they will turn over the roster.
The Dodgers shopped Teoscar Hernández last offseason, and they figure to do so again this offseason, as they already have a promising in-house replacement for him in left field in 21-year-old rookie Josue De Paula. Hernández has only one more guaranteed year remaining on his contract.
But what do the Dodgers do beyond that?
Do they attempt to move some of their other veterans? Or do they field more or less the same team next season, accept the limitations of their roster, and wait for some of their contracts to expire in another year?
Freeman will be an unrestricted free agent after the 2027 season. Muncy could also depart that winter, as his option for the 2028 season is a team option.
There are no simple answers.
Muncy’s option for 2028 is a relative bargain at $10 million, for example. The Dodgers might not be able to find a better third baseman at that price point.
Or, in the case of Freeman, how can they not re-sign a player as beloved as he is?
One factor that could influence the Dodgers’ team-building approach: Baseball’s next collective-bargaining agreement.
More restrictive spending limits of some kind figure to be on their way, as franchise owners are pushing for a salary cap. The Dodgers could be forced to dump salaries whether they want to or not.
Whatever happens on that front, the Dodgers will have to address Ohtani’s situation.
Ohtani broke into Japan’s top league as an 18 year old. He was a two-way player in the five seasons he played for the Nippon-Ham Fighters, and his body has plenty of mileage on it.
This season was particularly demanding.
Last year, resumed pitching in the middle of the season after recovering from his second major elbow operation. This year, he attempted to be a full-time hitter and pitcher for the entire season.
Ohtani broke down. He abandoned pitching in the middle of the season. The resulting injuries diminished him as a hitter.
Knowing Ohtani will insist on remaining a two-way player, what do the Dodgers do?
Do they spread out his starts to extend the periods between his starts? Or do they try to sell him on the idea that by not pitching in the early parts of the season, he could be a two-way player in October?
The results have spoken.
Changes will have to be made.

item.title: [FOX Sports] Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4
item.description: Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4 One loss from elimination, the Los Angeles Dodgers restored Shohei Ohtani to the top of the batting order for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night. The Dodgers trailed the Milwaukee Brewers 3-0 in the best-of-seven series, and needed to four straight wins to reach the World Series and keep alive their bid for a third consecutive championship. Ohtani batted sixth in a 6-2 loss on Wednesday
item.content:encoded:
Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4
One loss from elimination, the Los Angeles Dodgers restored Shohei Ohtani to the top of the batting order for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night.
The Dodgers trailed the Milwaukee Brewers 3-0 in the best-of-seven series, and needed to four straight wins to reach the World Series and keep alive their bid for a third consecutive championship.
Ohtani batted sixth in a 6-2 loss on Wednesday night, the lowest he's hit since joining the Dodgers ahead of the 2024 season. He was 1 for 2 with a walk to raise his batting average to .182.
"Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at," manager Dave Roberts said before the game. "I liked the at-bats yesterday. Obviously we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to."
(Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images)
Ohtani typically leads off the order but has been dropped lower while struggling with injuries to his left knee and right biceps for the last few months. Roberts didn't tell Ohtani about the change before posting the lineup.
Roberts said Ohtani has given him reasons to believe in the four-time MVP, citing Ohtani staying until 9 p.m. on Tuesday to work on his swing and his improved at-bat quality.
"Baking all that in, I felt absolutely, put him at the top," he said. "I feel good about him taking five at-bats and giving us our best chance to win and produce runs."
Roberts tweaked the entire lineup after Wednesday's loss put the Dodgers on the brink of elimination. Mookie Betts, who led off in Game 3, was bumped to No. 2, while Freddie Freeman moved to No. 3.
Will Smith, whose offensive struggles mirrored Ohtani's, moved up to fourth from seventh. Smith doubled in the sixth inning, when the Dodgers briefly took a 2-1 lead.
"I thought Will took very good at-bats, big hit yesterday," Roberts said. "He’s been in big spots."
Kyle Tucker hit fifth, while Teoscar Hernandez went from third to sixth. Miguel Rojas hit seventh and Andy Pages dropped to eighth from fifth.
Kiké Hernández, who came off the bench in Game 3, hit ninth, with regular third baseman Max Muncy available to come off the bench for Rojas or Kiké Hernández.
Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: [si.com] Brewers Are Using Postseason Stage to Showcase MLB’s New Era
item.dc:creator: Tom Verducci
item.description: Los Angeles — When dynasties fall, it is not insurrection, nor jealousy, nor sloth that bring them down. It is the undefeated champion of the world, Father Time. We are watching the Los Angeles Dodgers age out. The Milwaukee Brewers proved for a third time in the National League Championship Series they are the better (and younger) team, completing a beautiful triptych of comebacks with a 6-2 win in Game 3 on Wednesday. In three successive games, the Dodgers had Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles — When dynasties fall, it is not insurrection, nor jealousy, nor sloth that bring them down. It is the undefeated champion of the world, Father Time. We are watching the Los Angeles Dodgers age out.
The Milwaukee Brewers proved for a third time in the National League Championship Series they are the better (and younger) team, completing a beautiful triptych of comebacks with a 6-2 win in Game 3 on Wednesday. In three successive games, the Dodgers had Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Blake Snell on the mound with a lead and lost all three. Ninety-five million dollars, four Cy Young awards and a World Series MVP worth of pitching and they could not hold back Milwaukee any more than you can hold back water with your hands.
But the most obvious reason why the Brewers have put the Dodger dynasty on the brink of extinction is this: the youngest pitching staff in baseball—and the hardest throwing staff in postseason history—has smothered the oldest team in baseball. Milwaukee is pushing around the aging Dodgers lineup with a barrage of fastballs in three versions, especially power sinkers. They are shoving 66.8% fastballs at the Dodgers at an average velocity of 97.9 mph. The Dodgers’ only path to victory is to slug and the Brewers simply won’t allow it.
“I just think they’re really good pitchers,” Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas said. “A lot of their pitchers throw three different fastballs. They throw hard, and they’ve been locating the ball really well. They haven’t really given us too much of an opportunity to kind of build momentum.
“They’ve been attacking the zone. They throw their stuff in the zone—and with all three fastballs. A lot of guys have a cutter, a sinker and a four-seam fastball. It’s really hard to put barrels on the ball.
“At the end of the day, it’s just the velocity of their stuff. They throw the ball really hard. And we all know when you throw that hard, it’s really hard.”
The Brewers knew coming into the series that in today’s game older players don’t hit elite fastballs as well as younger players, and so the matchup was to their liking. But this? Who could have seen this in the NLCS? The Dodgers:
- Have two extra-base hits in 105 plate appearances
- Have been outhomered, 5-0
- Are the first team in franchise history to lose three straight games in one postseason with no home runs and no attempted stolen bases
- Are hitting .228 against fastballs
- Are 2-for-16 with runners in scoring position, part of a 3-for-32 postseason disaster in those spots
This has been the year in which baseball made a sharp turn when it comes to the speed of the game. Younger players thrive. Velocity, and the widespread adoption of the family of three fastballs, changed everything. You need fast-twitch athleticism, youthfulness. You need this generation of players who know velocity as a first language. You need rangy players on defense. The numbers bear out that younger players are the preferred way to go.
Players 30 and younger this year hit .247. Players in the 31-35 year-old demographic hit 10 points worse, .237, their worst showing ever. There was a time when front offices valued those 31-35 players because it seemed to be the peak intersection of experience and physical tools. Front offices were afraid to commit to younger players because of the lack of reps and track records. Those days are over.
The difference on the field in NLCS Game 3 was striking. The Brewers are the fastest team in baseball, as measured by sprint speed. The Dodgers are 24th.
The Brewers started a lineup and a pitcher with an average age of 26.1. They became the first team in history with a second postseason game starting three players 22 and younger: leftfielder Jackson Chourio, shortstop Cooper Pratt and rightfielder Luis Lara. Chourio opened the game with a first-pitch homer. Pratt smacked three hits, stole a base and scored a run. Lara flew around rightfield like a bird of prey, snaring anything that dared enter his airspace.
Watching Chourio, 22, Garrett Mitchell, 28, and Lara, 21, patrol the outfield was like watching an Olympic sprint relay team.
On the other side of the field, the Dodgers, especially their bats, looked old and slow. The average age of their starting 10 was 32.3 years old—more than six years older than Milwaukee’s fearless group. Only two starting Dodgers were in their 20s: centerfielder Andy Pages, 25, and Kyle Tucker, 29, who with his diminished range and baserunning has been trending older than his age.
By starting eight players 31 and older, these Dodgers joined the 2023 Dodgers, who got bounced by the Diamondbacks, as the only teams in the past 19 postseasons to trot out so many starting players that old in a game.
Fittingly, the old team played an outdated style of baseball, one from a generation ago. The ninth-place hitter, Tommy Edman, twice batted after the leadoff runner reached first base. Twice manager Dave Roberts did not ask him to bunt.
“I thought about it, but it’s just, he had a good pitch to hit. Flew out,” Roberts said. “I just didn’t feel giving up an out right there. Early in the game, I wanted Tommy to hit ...
“We haven’t been getting hits with runners in scoring position. To give up an out, to bank on getting a hit with runners in scoring position, I’d rather just try to maybe slug, hit a double.”
Edman was a below average hitter (97 OPS+) with a .385 slug this season.
Roberts and the Dodgers keep waiting for slug to show up at the expense of forfeiting the situational baseball as deployed by the other three remaining teams, the youthful Brewers, Guardians and Rays. The Dodgers still may be waiting Thanksgiving morning.
For instance, the Dodgers were down 1-0 in the sixth when Roberts sent 36-year-old Max Muncy to hit for Pages with runners on first and second and no outs. In that situation, the Brewers are bunting. Milwaukee plays get-em-over, get-em-in ball. The Dodgers? No way. Muncy is a three-true outcome guy. He is not going to bunt. Again, the Dodgers played for slug and got nothing. Muncy struck out. Will Smith, 31, did save the rally with a two-run double. But the Dodgers would go 1-for-12 after that against hard-throwing relievers D.L. Hall and Trevor Megill.
The lineup remained cold. Shohei Ohtani, 32, cannot pull a baseball because of lower-half injuries that won’t allow him to properly turn his hips and get to a firm front side. Freeman, 37, has three extra-base hits since Aug. 31.
“[Our] pitching staff has been great, to be honest,” Rojas said. “It’s really hard to put it into context when you have to pitch and have to play defense with a one run lead every single time. It’s like asking these guys to just throw a perfect inning every single time. It’s not sustainable. So, the blame is on the offense. We all know we could’ve done better, but nothing we can do now.”
How in the world has Milwaukee made Los Angeles look so bad?
“It’s pretty simple,” Muncy said. “We’ve played like [poop]. They’ve played great.”
Occam’s razor (or commode) aside, the one-sided NLCS is bigger than that. It stands as a changing of the guard, recalling the 1964 World Series, when the St. Louis Cardinals, emblematic of the National League embracing Black and Latin American players, ended the dynasty of an aging New York Yankees team, then the second oldest team in baseball. The younger, faster, harder-throwing, more creative team has been, beyond doubt, the better team.
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Max Muncy’s no-nonsense response to Dodgers’ performance doesn’t instill confidence for Game 4
item.dc:creator: Colin Keane

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are getting severely outplayed by the Milwaukee Brewers through the first three games of the National League Championship Series. LA's been outscored 15-7 so far in the series, and they've hit zero home runs to Milwaukee's five.
In Game 3, the Dodgers managed just five hits, failing to generate enough offense to compete with the Brewers' aggressive style. Jackson Chourio went yard on the first pitch of the game from Blake Snell. When LA seized the lead back in the sixth on a two-run double from Will Smith, Milwaukee bounced right back: In the next half inning, Jake Bauers and Garrett Mitchell hit back-to-back jacks off of Snell to re-take the lead.
The Brewers added additional runs in the eighth and ninth, whereas the Dodgers' bats didn't capitalize on opportunities to stay in the game (1-for-6 with runners in scoring position). Following the deflating result, Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy didn't exactly wax poetic about LA's struggles.
Max Muncy's blunt analysis of the Dodgers' struggles doesn't inspire faith for Game 4
Muncy's assessment of things is accurate, but it doesn't help Dodgers fans feel any better about Game 4 on Thursday night. It's admirable that Muncy chose to be honest rather than come up with some excuses for the Dodgers, but doing so also reinforced the harsh reality that LA simply might not be good enough right now to overcome what looks like a team of destiny over in the Brewers' dugout.
And there aren't excuses to make -- the Dodgers' stars are present, just not performing. Shohei Ohtani hasn't been himself, and it's not like LA's offense is without proven playoff performers like Mookie Betts and Freddie Freeman at the moment. Muncy's not helping matters, either, at least not in this series. After an awesome NLDS, Muncy is 1-for-9 with four strikeouts so far in the NLCS.
To keep their three-peat dream alive, the Dodgers must make history
If Muncy sounds pessimistic, it's probably because he understands the history of baseball. Only one team (the 2004 Boston Red Sox) has ever come back and won a best-of-seven series after trailing 3-0. It's never been done in an NLCS. If there's a group with the talent required to pull off the near-impossible, it's these Dodgers, but talent might not be the issue here.
The problem is momentum. The Brewers have scores of it, whereas the Dodgers look stuck in the mud. The other issue is that LA doesn't have any runway to generate the momentum they need. They are in the middle of a series and must act immediately or watch their season and three-peat hopes end just as swiftly.
Tyler Glasnow will surely put in a good performance in Game 4, but it won't mean anything if the Dodgers' offense is weak yet again. Muncy's simple assessment of things leads to a simple directive for the Dodgers: get on base early and often, and drive guys in when you do.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Pat Murphy's Managing Masterclass Outshines Dave Roberts, Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy
item.description: The 2026 National League Championship Series has been all Milwaukee Brewers so far. Milwaukee has a commanding three-game lead over the Los Angeles Dodgers with Game 4 scheduled to be played on Thursday night. If the Brewers win, they will advance to the World Series. There were many who thought the Brewers' streak of winning the National League Central would come to an end this season. Instead, the Brewers are on the doorstep of history. There are many reasons why Milwaukee has outplayed the Do
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 National League Championship Series has been all Milwaukee Brewers so far.
Milwaukee has a commanding three-game lead over the Los Angeles Dodgers with Game 4 scheduled to be played on Thursday night. If the Brewers win, they will advance to the World Series.
There were many who thought the Brewers' streak of winning the National League Central would come to an end this season. Instead, the Brewers are on the doorstep of history. There are many reasons why Milwaukee has outplayed the Dodgers throughout the series. The bullpen has been incredible, Jake Bauers has shined and the rotation has done its job. One guy who deserves a lot of credit is Pat Murphy, as well.
There's a reason why he's the two-time reigning National League Manager of the Year and should win the award again. Murphy has pushed all of the right buttons throughout the NLCS. Between the Brewers and the Dodgers, the NLCS has two of the best managers in the game in Murphy and Dave Roberts. Of the two, Murphy has clearly been the best this series, though.
The Brewers Are Sitting Pretty
It seems like every single decision the Brewers have made this series has been the right one. In Game 2, the Brewers put David Hamilton in the starting lineup and he went 2-for-3 with three runs scored and two stolen bases. That was a game-changer. In Game 1, the Brewers had Luis Lara in the starting lineup and he drove in what would end up being the game-winning run for Milwaukee. In Game 3, the Brewers started the game with Christian Yelich, Sal Frelick and Hamilton all on the bench. Andrew Vaughn, who replaced Yelich in the lineup, drew an important walk in the seventh inning. Then, Yelich pinch-ran for him and was driven in by Bauers' two-run homer.
Ortiz, who was at third base over Hamilton, drove in a run during the Game 3 win as well. Plus, the Brewers have gotten seemingly every pitching decision right. The starters haven't gone deep and Milwaukee has known exactly when to turn it over to the bullpen. On the other hand, Roberts made what could be argued as a few mistakes, specifically in Game 3. Andy Pages was yanked in favor of Max Muncy. Prized rookie Josue De Paula was wasted in Game 3 as well and was replaced by Kiké Hernandez at a critical point in the game. Plus, the offense in general has done nothing.
Milwaukee has pushed all of the right buttons, whereas the Dodgers have faltered. This is absolutely a testament to Murphy, as well as the players on the field.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding "Milwaukee Brewers On SI," please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.title: [Yardbarker] Max Muncy & Andy Pages Named Gold Glove Award Finalists 2026
item.dc:creator: This article first appeared; Was Syndicated
item.description: Rawlings Gold Glove Award finalists for the National League and American League were announced, with the Los Angeles Dodgers having Max Muncy (third base) and Andy Pages (center field) placing among the top-three finishers at their respective positions. The 2026 season marks a fifth consecutive year in which the Dodgers have had multiple Gold Glove Award finalists. Mookie Betts (shortstop) and Miguel Rojas (utility) were last season’s representatives. From 2022-24, the Dodgers have had seven oth
item.content:encoded:
Rawlings Gold Glove Award finalists for the National League and American League were announced, with the Los Angeles Dodgers having Max Muncy (third base) and Andy Pages (center field) placing among the top-three finishers at their respective positions.
The 2026 season marks a fifth consecutive year in which the Dodgers have had multiple Gold Glove Award finalists. Mookie Betts (shortstop) and Miguel Rojas (utility) were last season’s representatives.
From 2022-24, the Dodgers have had seven other nominees. Betts has been the only Dodgers player to win a Gold Glove since 2022, as he took home the hardware for right field that year.
Gold Glove Award winners for the nine standard positions are determined via vote of MLB managers and up to six coaches from each team. Managers and coaches cannot vote for their own players and are only permitted to submit ballots for those in their same league.
Those votes amount to 75% of the selection total, with the SABR Defensive Index accounting for the remaining 25%.
The Toronto Blue Jays and Chicago Cubs had an MLB-best five players named finalists, with the Atlanta Braves, Arizona Diamondbacks, Texas Rangers and Kansas City Royals close behind at four apiece.
All 2026 Gold Glove Award winners will be announced live on ESPN on Sunday, Nov. 1.
For Muncy, it is his second career Gold Glove nomination and his first as a third baseman.
It is an impressive accomplishment for Muncy, improving his defense to such an extent in his age 36 season. He is looking to win his first career Gold Glove Award after falling short as a first baseman in 2021.
Alex Bregman (Chicago Cubs) and Javier Sanoja (Marlins) are the other two finalists.
Pages has been one of the best defensive center fielders in baseball since his breakout 2025 season.
In just his third season, he has already collected his first individual award this season as a representative in the Fall Classic.
It would be the first Gold Glove of his career if he can secure the votes. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts foresaw this outcome for the 25-year-old at the midpoint of the season.
Pages arm has arguably been his best weapon on defense this season, as he led the league with 13 outfield assists.
He is facing some stiff competition, with Pete Crow-Armstrong and Michael Harris II also up for consideration.

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers are one loss away from getting swept in the postseason for the first time since the 2023 NLDS against the Diamondbacks. No matter how you want to slice it, they’ve looked inferior in every facet of the game in this series, from situational hitting to defense, bullpen work, and so on—now it’ll be up to Tyler Glasnow to at the very least delay what appears to be an unavoidable postseason exit for the reigning back-to-back champs.
Although the Brewers have yet to formally announce a starter, all signs point towards Dustin May taking the ball in Game 4 of this series—it might be with an opener, or it might be with him as a starter; either way, the bulk innings role will belong to the former Dodger.
When it comes to lineup decisions, Max Muncy figures to regain a starting role at third base, and you have to wonder if Will Smith remains in the seventh spot—the Dodger catcher was responsible for the only big hit the home team had in a Game 3 loss. Speaking of hitters who moved down in the order, although it amounted to very little, Shohei Ohtani reached safely in three of his four plate appearances in a 6-2 defeat.
Neither Evan Phillips nor Roki Sasaki had especially lengthy appearances off the bullpen, so apart from Justin Wrobleski, there’ll be no one else unavailable in the bullpen for Game 4. With nothing to lose and following the seventh-inning debacle of leaving Blake Snell in too long, expect potential aggressive calls to the bullpen at the first sign of trouble for Glasnow.
NLCS Game 4 info
- Teams: No. 2 seed Dodgers vs. No. 1 seed Brewers
- Series: Milwaukee leads, 3-0
- Ballpark: Dodger Stadium, Los Angeles
- Start time: 5:08 p.m.
- TV: FS1 (Joe Davis, John Smoltz, Ken Rosenthal, Tom Verducci)
- National radio: ESPN Radio (Jon Sciambi, Doug Glanville)
- Local English radio: AM 570 (Charley Steiner, Rick Monday)
- Local Spanish radio: KTNQ 1020 AM (José Mota, Luis Cruz)

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Max Muncy Puts Dodgers' Problems Plainly
item.dc:creator: Cameron Kiszla
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are now down 3-0 to the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series, and Dodgers veteran Max Muncy knows exactly why that is. Wednesday night was a frustrating loss in which the Dodgers finally seemed to fix their offensive woes, only for star pitcher Blake Snell to implode with back-to-back home runs in the seventh inning. Max Muncy sounds off on the Dodgers Muncy, the third baseman, was asked by reporters what has been going on with the team’s offensive
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are now down 3-0 to the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series, and Dodgers veteran Max Muncy knows exactly why that is.
Wednesday night was a frustrating loss in which the Dodgers finally seemed to fix their offensive woes, only for star pitcher Blake Snell to implode with back-to-back home runs in the seventh inning.
Max Muncy sounds off on the Dodgers
Muncy, the third baseman, was asked by reporters what has been going on with the team’s offensive struggles, and he pulled no punches.
“It’s a pretty simple answer. We’re playing like s—. They’re playing great,” he said, as reported by the California Post’s Jack Harris and other reporters.
In case you think Muncy is being hyperbolic, he’s not.
As detailed by Newsweek baseball writer J.P. Hoornstra, the Dodgers are one of 274 teams too play at least seven postseason games in a season since 1903.
Their team OPS of .572 isn’t just in the lower end of that group; it’s almost dead last.
The 2026 Dodgers are 268th, meaning only six teams have had a worse OPS in more than a century.
It’s a far cry from the powerful lineup fans expected from the back-to-back World Series champions.
In fact, the Dodgers haven’t hit a home run at all in this series against the Brewers, despite boasting power hitters like Muncy, Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman and plenty of others.
What’s next for the Dodgers?
The Dodgers will try to avoid “playing like s—” for a fourth straight game on Thursday, knowing that a loss will end their season.
Tyler Glasnow is the mound for the Boys in Blue as they look to avoid the sweep.
The game will begin at 5 p.m. PT, an hour earlier than the previously announced start time of 6 p.m. PT.
Pitcher Blake Snell, who started Game 3 and gave up a pair of back-breaking home runs in the seventh inning, told reporters the team is focused on winning Thursday’s game.
“Yeah, it sucks, but it’s part of it,” he said. “How do we bounce back, how do we fight? I think that’s the most important thing, us coming together and finding a way to win.”
Do you think the Dodgers can stave off elimination on Thursday?

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Max Muncy gives blunt assessment of Dodgers' performance vs. Brewers in NLCS: 'We're playing like s***'
item.dc:creator: Chris Cwik
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are suddenly in big trouble. After yet another loss Wednesday, the Dodgers find themselves down 3-0 in the National League Championship Series. With another loss, they'll be eliminated from the postseason. This wasn't the way it was supposed to be. In year's past, the Dodgers' depth and financial muscle won out against the best teams in the game. Something is different this time around and Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy thinks he knows exactly what's going on. When asked
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are suddenly in big trouble. After yet another loss Wednesday, the Dodgers find themselves down 3-0 in the National League Championship Series. With another loss, they'll be eliminated from the postseason.
This wasn't the way it was supposed to be. In year's past, the Dodgers' depth and financial muscle won out against the best teams in the game. Something is different this time around and Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy thinks he knows exactly what's going on.
When asked, Muncy summed things up succinctly saying, "We're playing like s***."
"It's a pretty simple answer: We're playing like s*** they're playing great."
Max Muncy after the Dodgers dropped Game 3 of the NLCS. pic.twitter.com/0MRmqhpnDk
— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 15, 2026
Muncy, of course, made sure to give the Milwaukee Brewers credit. After lamenting his own team's struggles, Muncy added, "[The Brewers] are playing great. It's as simple as that."
Much has been made of the struggles of Dodgers two-way star Shohei Ohtani this postseason, but he wasn't the problem Wednesday. After being dropped to sixth in the batting order, Ohtani reached base three times in the contest.
His overall numbers, however, are still a problem, as Ohtani is hitting just .182 in the series. Many of his teammates have similar batting averages, including Freddie Freeman, Teoscar Hernandez and Muncy, none of whom is hitting above .192. Catcher Will Smith is hitting under .100.
While those struggles can be written off as small-sample outcomes … the NLCS is a small sample. All it takes is a few bad games from your star players to decide the outcome of a series. The Dodgers are experiencing that phenomenon right now.
Because of that, though, it won't take much for the Dodgers to claw their way back into the series. While 3-0 comebacks are highly unlikely, they are not impossible. All it would take is the Dodgers' stars hitting like they should.
Even then, that might not be enough. In order to stage a comeback, the Dodgers also need the Brewers to give them an opening, which seems unlikely given how well Milwaukee is playing right now.

item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
Blake Snell stood on the mound with his hand on his hip, waiting for Jake Bauers to cross the plate before punching in his pitch call for the next batter.
The Dodgers left-hander had just given up the lead on Bauers’ two-run homer, spoiling what had been a stellar start Wednesday night at Dodger Stadium. But Snell was ready to move on.
Two pitches later, he watched another ball fly over the fence, this time off Garrett Mitchell’s bat.
The Dodgers’ 6-2 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, after the visitors regained the lead with back-to-back home runs in the seventh inning, gave the Brewers a commanding 3-0 lead and set up an elimination game Thursday. After setting their sights on a history-making three-peat, the Dodgers will have to win the next four games just to advance to the World Series.
The Dodgers showed signs of life during Game 3 of the NLCS, but Bill Plaschke writes the reigning champs can’t survive their crushing collapse.
For five innings, the only run on the board was the one the Brewers scored on the first pitch of the game.
Snell zipped a 97.6-mph fastball over the center of the plate, and Brewers leadoff hitter Jackson Chourio sent it into the first row of the stands in right-center.
For much of Snell’s start, however, that aggressive approach worked. He dotted the upper rail with his fastball, threw his curveball for both swings and misses and called strikes, and mixed in his changeup to right-handed batters.
Unlike Snell’s last postseason start, when he issued five walks and lasted just 3-2/3 innings against the Atlanta Braves, his efficiency got him through six-plus innings Wednesday, with just two walks.
And while Snell’s fastball averaged 97 mph in his last start — something he’d done only twice before in his career, regular season or postseason, and not since 2022, according to Statcast — he threw even harder on Wednesday: 97.3 mph.
After Chourio’s home run, Snell retired 18 of the next 20 batters, including 14 in a row, to get through six innings. His nine strikeouts were one shy of a postseason career high, which he recorded against the Brewers last year in Game 1 of the NLCS.
Then in the seventh inning, he issued a leadoff walk to Andrew Vaughn and surrendered back-to-back homers, and suddenly the game had flipped.
With the way the Brewers’ bullpen pitched in the first two games, it seemed the Dodgers would have to score against the Brewers’ starters to have a chance to pull themselves out of the hole they’d dug.
They failed to do so in Game 3, logging just three hits off left-hander Robert Gasser.
Luckily for them, pitching every game of the postseason seemed to finally have caught up to hard-throwing right-handed Abner Uribe in his seventh appearance.
Uribe took over for Gasser in the sixth inning and walked the first two batters he faced.
Then Dodgers manager Dave Roberts had left-handed-hitting Max Muncy pinch-hit for Andy Pages. Muncy struck out, and the biggest moment of the game fell to two Dodgers who have had the worst postseason production on the team.
Roberts had moved Shohei Ohtani down to sixth in the batting order and put Will Smith behind him. Naturally, the game found them.
Ohtani drew a five-pitch walk without taking a swing. With the bases loaded, it was up to Smith, who had gone one for 25 in the postseason to that point.
He ambushed a first-pitch sinker and drove it into the left-field gap for a two-run double and the lead.
The rally halted there. Roberts burned rookie Josue De Paula as a pinch-hitter, swapping him out for Kiké Hernández when the Brewers brought in left-hander DL Hall. Hernández and Tommy Edman struck out to end the inning.
The Dodgers could not keep pace with the Milwaukee Brewers, falling 6-2 Wednesday night in Game 3 of the NLCS and dropping to 3-0 in the series.
Then, three Brewers batters into the seventh, the Dodgers were down 4-2.
Snell hadn’t allowed a home run all year — not in his nine regular-season starts, or in his NLDS appearance. Three on Wednesday defined his start.
The next inning, the Brewers added an insurance run with back-to-back singles against right-handed reliever Roki Sasaki and a wild pitch from left-hander Justin Wrobleski. They tacked on another in the ninth with a pair of singles and a stolen base off Wrobleski.
With the flash of red tail lights flickering outside of the stadium, a sign of Dodgers fans already heading for the exits, Dodgers hitters went down in order in the final half inning.

item.title: [Orange County Register] Brewers push Dodgers to the brink, hit 3 homers off Blake Snell for 3-0 NLCS lead
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett

The plucky little team that doesn’t hit home runs hit three of them off of Blake Snell on Wednesday night. The Milwaukee Brewers handed the Dodgers a 6-2 defeat in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, pushing the back-to-back champions to the brink of elimination with the possibility of a sweep to avenge the one the Dodgers handed them last year. “It’s a pretty simple answer,” Max Muncy said when as
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Reach out and feel the drywall. The Dodgers’ backs are up against it.
The plucky little team that doesn’t hit home runs hit three of them off of Blake Snell on Wednesday night. The Milwaukee Brewers handed the Dodgers a 6-2 defeat in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, pushing the back-to-back champions to the brink of elimination with the possibility of a sweep to avenge the one the Dodgers handed them last year.
“It’s a pretty simple answer,” Max Muncy said when asked how the Dodgers find themselves in this position. “We’re playing like (profanity). They’re playing great. It’s as simple as that. No need to overcomplicate it.”
Dreams of a three-peat on life support, the Dodgers’ thoughts now have to be on a ‘four-peat’ – it will take four consecutive victories for them to become just the second team in MLB history to come back from a 3-0 deficit to win a best-of-seven series. The 2004 Boston Red Sox (featuring a key stolen base by a reserve outfielder acquired at midseason from the Dodgers) did it in the American League Championship Series against the New York Yankees.
“If we lose, we’re done. We’ve got to go on one-game winning streaks four games in a row,” Kike’ Hernandez said.
“At the beginning of this year, we set out to do something historic,” Muncy said. “It looks like we’re going to have to make a little more history along the way if we want to accomplish that. That’s the task ahead of us. We still have the pitching staff to be able to do it. We just have to get some hits. If we can back our pitching staff then I know that, like I said, we have the pitching staff to do it.”
Tyler Glasnow is scheduled to start Game 4 on Thursday and try to save the Dodgers’ season. Muncy is correct — Glasnow won’t be able to do it without someone applying paddles to the Dodgers’ flatlining offense.
The Dodgers might not be going down without a fight. But so far, they are going down without any of the things it takes to make an offense successful in the postseason.
They are 2 for 16 with runners in scoring position in this series, 3 for 32 in the postseason. They have just two two-out hits in the three NLCS games (both singles) and only two extra-base hits (both doubles). The Dodgers hit 204 home runs in the regular season (tied for fourth in the National League) and eight more in their four-game National League Division Series victory over the Atlanta Braves (the most in the postseason to that point). They have hit none in the NLCS.
“They’re really good pitchers,” Miguel Rojas said. “A lot of their pitchers throw three different fastballs. They throw hard. They’ve been locating the ball really well. They haven’t really given us too many opportunities to build momentum.
“They’ve been attacking the zone. They trust their stuff in the zone. With all three fastballs, with a lot of guys that have a cutter, a sinker and a four-seam fastball, it’s really hard to kind of put barrels on the ball. So you’ve got to build some momentum that you can create with hits, but we haven’t been able to get a big hit.”
The Brewers have grabbed any momentum right back from the Dodgers. The Dodgers have scored in just five of the 27 innings so far. Four of those five times, the Brewers responded by scoring in the next half-inning themselves.
It happened again to turn Game 3.
Snell hadn’t give up a home run this year but Jackson Chourio sent the first pitch he threw Wednesday into the right-field pavilion. Snell thoroughly dominated the Brewers through six innings after that. He retired 18 of 20 batters after Chourio’s home run, striking out nine. Through the first five innings, the Brewers swung at 32 of Snell’s pitches and missed (17) more times than they made contact.
But the Dodgers’ lifeless offense did nothing against the Brewers’ second consecutive rookie starter, Robert Gasser, who held them scoreless on three hits and a walk through five innings.
Brewers manager Pat Murphy went to his bullpen after that, calling on Abner Uribe for the seventh time in their seven postseason games. When Uribe took the mound, the Brewers’ relievers had pitched 9⅔ scoreless innings in the NLCS and had allowed just one earned run in 28⅔ innings this postseason.
But Uribe walked the bases loaded, retiring just one batter. That brought up Will Smith – 1 for his first 25 this postseason. Smith jumped on a first-pitch fastball from Uribe and lined it off the wall in left-center field for a two-run double and a 2-1 lead.
It was the kind of clutch hit that Smith has provided time and time again over the years and had the stadium rocking.
Murphy made his next move, bringing in left-hander DL Hall with runners at second and third. Hall struck out pinch-hitter Kiké Hernandez and Tommy Edman as the Dodgers failed to capitalize on a chance to break the game open.
Snell went back out for the seventh inning having retired 14 in a row. But he walked Andrew Vaughn to start the inning and bring up Jake Bauers whose 12-pitch walk in the third inning of Game 2 was a critical turning point against Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He did it again, extending his at-bat against Snell for 11 pitches and sending the last one, a fastball over the heart of the plate, into the right-field seats for a two-run home run. Two pitches later, Snell floated a changeup over the middle and Garrett Mitchell sent it on the same flight path as Bauers’ drive.
In 1,200⅔ career innings (regular season), Snell has only given up 15 home runs to left-handed hitters. Bauers and Mitchell did it back-to-back. The Brewers hit 154 home runs during the regular season, the fewest in the National League. They have outhomered the Dodgers 5-0 in the NLCS.
“I mean three home runs in a game — I didn’t give up one the whole year,” Snell said. “To have three in a game is pretty frustrating.”
The Brewers added single runs in the eighth and ninth innings to pull away.

Will Smith Becomes Dad to Third Child!!
Just moments before the pivotal Game 3 against the Brewers, Will Smith's wife, Cara, announced a major piece of life news for the Smith family.
She has successfully given birth to her and Will's third child!
Here is the post the two share on Instagram, and they hint that their new daughter's name is 'Carter':
Perhaps this huge piece of life news can get Will Smith going at the plate in the NLCS, as the Dodgers' 2025 World Series hero has slumped since the beginning of the MLB playoffs.
Perhaps being at home will help wake Will Smith regardless.
However, either way, huge congrats to the Smith family for adding a new member to their growing family.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Quietly Announce Roster News on 6-Year MLB Player
Taking a Quick Look at Will Smith's MLB Career
Will Smith is a 3X World Series champion with the Los Angeles Dodgers. He's also been named to the MLB All-Star team three times.
Since making his MLB debut in 2019, Smith has spent his entire 8-year career with the Dodgers.
Over 795 total games played in his career, Smith has 138 home runs, 137 doubles, 476 RBI, and a lifetime OPS+ of 127.
He's been a lifeline for the Dodgers offense in many big moments in his career, and the Dodgers will continue to call his name during the playoffs.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dave Roberts Explain Dodgers' Lineup Shuffle for Game 3
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb

Kyle Tucker moves to cleanup, Will Smith bats seventh, and Miguel Rojas starts against left-hander Robert Gasser, with Max Muncy available off the bench. With the Dodgers down 2–0, he also spoke about Ohtani’s late-night work and the intens
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Shohei Ohtani will hit sixth Wednesday as Dave Roberts reshapes the Dodgers’ lineup for Game 3 against Milwaukee. Kyle Tucker moves to cleanup, Will Smith bats seventh, and Miguel Rojas starts against left-hander Robert Gasser, with Max Muncy available off the bench. Roberts said the changes give the order better balance and make it tougher for Milwaukee to work through its pitching matchups. With the Dodgers down 2–0, he also spoke about Ohtani’s late-night work and the intensity he expects from starter Blake Snell.
“Shohei’s all on board”
Roberts sees Tucker as a good fit in the middle of the order against both Gasser and the relievers who may follow him.
“I love the length of the lineup,” Roberts said. “Kyle has been, throughout his career and currently, agnostic with pitchers left versus right. Gasser is a guy they’re probably going to run two times through the lineup. If it gets a little beyond that, I like Kyle there.”
Smith moves down again after batting fifth in Game 2. Roberts hopes a different spot will help the catcher’s at-bats fall into place.
“Give the player a different look, let the game come to him,” he said. “Last game, there were some good swings in there, which I’m really encouraged about. Having him there around the wraparound of the lineup, I think, is going to be a good thing.”
“I’ve got Miggy in there, which I’m excited about, having Miggy versus a left-hander and then deploying Max whenever the time makes sense.”
Ohtani’s move is part of that effort to spread out the left-handed and right-handed bats.
“It’s more what gives our lineup the best balance,” Roberts said. “Separating the lefties, the righties, making it a little more difficult for them to navigate our lineup. Shohei’s all on board. Whatever it takes to win.”
Ohtani puts in the work
Roberts said Ohtani stayed late Tuesday to work on his swing and talk with teammates about beating Milwaukee.
“As far as him as a person, he couldn’t be more of a team player, more agreeable,” Roberts said. “He was here late last night working on his swing, out with the guys and talking about things, how we’re going to beat these guys.”
“God, it couldn’t be more of a joy. This guy is great for our game. He’s great for all of us.”
Roberts saw a sharper focus in that work.
“He expects a lot from himself, obviously, and he hasn’t performed to his expectations,” he said. “It’s up to all of us to do our jobs. But this was a different look from Shohei yesterday.”
“He was determined, and that’s an understatement.”
Snell’s “slow burn”
Snell gets the ball after a disappointing NLDS start against Atlanta. Roberts has noticed a quieter pitcher waiting for his next chance.
“Much more quiet, staying to himself more,” he said. “He’s been really anxious to get another opportunity. Still being a part of the team and cheering for guys, but this has been a slow burn since that last outing.”
“When you see him take the mound today, you’re going to see another level of intensity. For me, it’s making sure you manage that intensity because it’s already a big game.”
Roberts also likes the thought Snell has put into understanding Milwaukee’s approach.
“He’s a very cerebral, thoughtful person,” Roberts said. “To understand the psyche of your opponent is important because it adds to his edge, his focus, knowing how hungry and feisty and tough that team is.”
“Being aggressive to match their intensity, I like that exercise and what he’s been doing.”
Make the relievers work
Roberts wants more sustained at-bats against a Brewers bullpen that has held the Dodgers scoreless through two games.
“Mookie’s done a good job of still winning pitches, competing in at-bats,” he said. “Other guys, we’ve got to have that same level of fight against those guys versus one-, two-pitch outs.”
“Ashby has been very efficient against us. You’ve got to go through the pain of an at-bat, the grind of it, to ultimately have those guys make a mistake. We could do a better job of that.”
Betts’ work has stood out beyond his batting line.
“He’s playing really high-level baseball,” Roberts said. “If you watch the games, he’s seeing a ton of pitches. He’s getting on base. He’s moving guys over, and that’s what you have to do to win playoff games.”
“There are a couple more big hits in there, maybe a homer. I love the way he’s playing. He’s in a good frame of mind right now, and he’s playing next-level shortstop as well.”
Everything goes into tonight
Roberts plans to manage Game 3 with the urgency its place in the series demands.
“We still have to win four games, but the most important game is tonight,” he said. “We’re going to do everything we can to win this one, and our guys understand how important this one is.”
“It’s good to be home. Those guys fed off their crowd, and I’m excited to see some blue towels and some noise tonight and have our guys feed off it.”
For Roberts, keeping the focus on one game also helps keep the task manageable.
“Guys love to compete. I love to compete,” he said. “We all know what’s at stake. It’s going to be fun. There’s some pressure there, but you’ve got to embrace this.”
“When you start thinking about winning four games, I get nervous. But I think we can manage winning a game tonight.”

item.content:encoded:
The NLCS resumes at Dodger Stadium on Wednesday, with the Dodgers looking to embark on a comeback down 2-0 in the series against the Milwaukee Brewers.
The top three in the lineup remain the same, as Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman and Teoscar Hernández hit in the top three spots. The middle of the lineup received an adjustment that comes as little to no surprise with how Shohei Ohtani and Will Smith have hit in the postseason.
Kyle Tucker moves up to cleanup in the starting lineup, the highest spot in the order he's been placed in this October. After a rough regular season, Tucker has found his stride at the plate at the bottom of the lineup, slashing .300/.391/.500 with a home run and two RBI over six games. Tucker has faced Milwaukee's Game 3 starter Robert Gasser twice in his career, collecting three hits across six at-bats including a home run.
Andy Pages has also impressed at the plate this postseason, turning the page on what was a historically awful title run at the plate last year. The 2026 All-Star has five hits across 20 at-bats, with his highlights being his go-ahead, two-run single in Game 4 of the NLDS and for getting the Dodgers on the board against Jacob Misiorowski in Game 1 of the NLCS. Pages has gone hitless since his Game 1 RBI single, but he moves up to fifth in the lineup against Gasser, also the highest spot he's hit in the postseason this year.
The elephant in the room is Shohei Ohtani getting moved all the way down to sixth in the lineup. Ohtani was adamant about playing in Game 3, and Dave Roberts ultimately granted his wish.
"He's adamant he feels good enough to be in there. He's close to finding something with his swing. I feel great about it," manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday just before the Dodgers workout at Dodger Stadium. "He was very convicted that he is onto something mechanically. He was adamant that he can help us. He's well enough to help us win a baseball game. So that's all I needed to hear."
Try as he might to will his way into the lineup, Ohtani has been a detriment offensively since hitting his final regular season home run on Aug. 18 in Denver, and he's carried that funk over the team's six playoff games slashing just .150/.261/.150 with zero RBI. Ohtani had never hit as low as second in the lineup until Game 3 of the NLDS, and it's the first time Ohtani is hitting sixth in the lineup since Sept. 19, 2020 back when he was with the Angels.
Will Smith has also struggled mightily this October, and he slides all the way down to seventh in the starting lineup. Miguel Rojas gets the start at third base over Max Muncy against the left-hander Gasser, and Tommy Edman gets the start at second base, rounding things out in the lineup. Blake Snell makes his first start since getting the ball for Game 2 of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are facing a must-win in Game Three of the NLCS against the Milwaukee Brewers on Wednesday evening.
The good news for the Dodgers is that the series is shifting back to Los Angeles. Blake Snell will get the start for LA on Wednesday evening, and he will oppose Robert Gasser.
Before the game started, the Dodgers announced their Game Three lineup, which featured a major Will Smith decision.
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Announce Blake Snell News Before Pivotal Brewers Game
Will Smith Dropped in Los Angeles Dodgers Batting Order
When the Dodgers Game Three lineup dropped on Wednesday afternoon, it came with a few surprises.
In two big developments, Will Smith and Shohei Ohtani have dropped in the batting order.
Here is the full group, per @UnderdogMLB:
Dodgers 10/14: “M. Betts SS F. Freeman 1B T. Hernández LF K. Tucker RF A. Pages CF S. Ohtani DH W. Smith C M. Rojas 3B T. Edman 2B B. Snell SP”
The flip to Will Smith being demoted in the lineup is that Kyle Tucker has moved up several spots and will bat cleanup against the Brewers’ LHP Gasser.
Shohei Ohtani bats sixth, and Tommy Edman/Miguel Rojas are getting starts in the infield, while Max Muncy gets the pine.
More MLB on Heavy: Toronto Blue Jays Predicted to Poach Yankees All-Star for $80 Million
Taking a Quick Look at Will Smith’s 2026 Season
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – MAY 08: Will Smith #16 of the Los Angeles Dodgers during a 3-1 win over the Atlanta Braves at Dodger Stadium on May 08, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images)
As did many of the Los Angeles Dodgers (at some point in 2026), Will Smith spent a good chunk of time on the Injured List with a neck issue.
He got a handful of starts down the stretch of the regular season, but he’s been really struggling at the plate in the MLB playoffs, and after moving him down for Game Two, manager Dave Roberts is now demoting him to the 7-spot in the lineup.
Perhaps it’s a wake-up call for Smith, but as the Dodgers search for the right lineup combination, having Smith (who is 1-for-20+) in the 3-hole just isn’t going to get things going.
It will be interesting to see if this decision pays off for Roberts and the rest of the Dodgers.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Issued Strong Anthony Volpe Take Amid Major Decision

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers' Muncy, Pages Named 2026 Gold Glove Finalists
item.dc:creator: Jordon Lawrenz
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to avoid being swept in the National League Championship Series, and that starts in Game 3, which takes place on Wednesday, the same day when the Gold Glove Award finalists were revealed. The likes of Mookie Betts, Teoscar Hernandez, Kyle Tucker, and even Yoshinobu Yamamoto weren't named finalists, but Andy Pages and Max Muncy were. Pages represents the Dodgers in center field while Muncy is their third base representative. Both players have their work cut out
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to avoid being swept in the National League Championship Series, and that starts in Game 3, which takes place on Wednesday, the same day when the Gold Glove Award finalists were revealed.
The likes of Mookie Betts, Teoscar Hernandez, Kyle Tucker, and even Yoshinobu Yamamoto weren't named finalists, but Andy Pages and Max Muncy were.
Pages represents the Dodgers in center field while Muncy is their third base representative.
Both players have their work cut out for them, but even being named one of three NL finalists is a huge accomplishment for how grueling a 162-game season is.
Dodgers face stiff odds for Muncy to win
Muncy is officially a Gold Glove finalist for the second time in his career, but it seems like he's going to need to try again next year.
The three-time All-Star is matched up against Alex Bregman, one of the best defenders in all of baseball, and Javier Sanoja.
MLB.com made note that Muncy hasn't been a plus defender by fielding run value since 2021, and that's something that Bregman has been doing on a consistent basis.
Here in 2026, Bregman notched his seventh straight season of being an above-average defender, and the 2024 Gold Glove Award winner ended the year with +9 outs above average.
For reference, that was second among all third basemen. Sanoja has a case to be made with his +6 OAA, which is fourth in the NL, along with his +5 FRV, which was tied for fourth.
Sanoja won the Gold Glove Award last year as a utility player, but now is stuck at third base where both he and Muncy will likely fall to Bregman.
Pages is stuck against Pete Crow-Armstrong
Is there a worse person to be going up against than Pete Crow-Armstrong? The likely 2026 NL MVP had a defensive value worth +23 runs, which led the league.
PCA's OAA came in at +26, which is officially the highest by an outfielder in a single season this decade.
Pages sported a strong +13 FRV, which was the third most among qualified outfielders, but it was still nothing in comparison to Crow-Armstrong's +26.
Sure, Pages led the league with 14 outfield assists, but it seems like a foregone conclusion that PCA will be leaving with the hardware on Sunday, Nov. 1.
Michael Harris II was the third finalist. He put together a career year with his +14 OAA and +12 FRV.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers hope to punch back in the NLCS with a home win in Game 3 over the Milwaukee Brewers.
The Dodgers are down 0-2 in the series, but hope isn’t lost; this Dodgers team thrives when it’s backed into a corner. To turn things around, the offense needs to convert on scoring chances.
Dodgers’ Lineup vs. Brewers
1. Mookie Betts, SS
2. Freddie Freeman, 1B
3. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
4. Kyle Tucker, RF
5. Andy Pages, CF
6. Shohei Ohtani, DH
7. Will Smith, C
8. Miguel Rojas, 3B
9. Tommy Edman, 2B
The Dodgers announced Tuesday that Shohei Ohtani will play despite his struggles and injuries. He will stay in the 6-hole, his lowest spot yet for the Dodgers.
The Brewers are rolling out lefty Robert Gasser, who possesses some matchup problems. Naturally, right-handers Teoscar Hernandez and Andy Pages are moving up from their usual positions.
Will Smith, who has also struggled in the postseason, is moving down to his lowest spot in a while.
Other than shuffling players around, Roberts is sticking with the same group from Game 2, with the only exception being Miguel Rojas at third base while Max Muncy sits.
Who is pitching for the Dodgers?
Blake Snell takes the mound for the Dodgers in the biggest spot of his career. The team needs him to deliver a great outing to keep their three-peat hopes alive against a game Brewers team.
Snell has posted a 1.90 ERA over 42.2 innings this year. In the postseason, he hasn’t been as sharp in one start. He pitched just 3.2 innings in Game 2 of the NLDS, allowing one run but giving up five walks and three hits.
Against this crop of Brewers hitters, they’re hitting only 11-for-64 with a .172 average, a .274 OBP, and 29 strikeouts.
If Snell does well in this game, his legacy as a Dodger and pitcher will grow exponentially.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Andy Pages and Max Muncy Named Gold Glove Finalists for 2026
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — Max Muncy and Andy Pages have given Dodgers fans something to celebrate on the defensive side of the ball. Both are among the Gold Glove finalists announced so far, recognition that puts their gloves in the spotlight while Los Angeles fights to keep its postseason run going.
