item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have had plenty of postseason heroes during their World Series runs in 2024 and 2025.
Last year, the biggest may have been backup infielder Miguel Rojas, who hit a game-tying home run in Game 7 against the Toronto Blue Jays in the ninth inning.
As a result, Rojas has continued to get opportunities in 2026 and was inserted into the starting lineup for Game 3 against the Atlanta Braves in this year's NLDS. He also started Game 2 in place of Max Muncy at third base.
Oct 6, 2026; Cumberland, Georgia, USA; ]Los Angeles Dodgers second baseman Miguel Rojas (72) throws to first base for an out against the Atlanta Braves during the first inning in game three of the NLDS for the 2026 MLB Playoffs at Truist Park. Mandatory Credit: Brett Davis-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
Rojas was put in to hit against Braves left-hander Chris Sale given his platoon advantage as a right-handed hitter. It did not work out through his first three at-bats as he went 0-for-3 with a strikeout.
Rojas remained in the game for a fourth at-bat in the eighth inning against Braves reliever Brent Suter, who is also a southpaw.
Unfortunately, he did not finish the at-bat. After fouling off the second pitch he immediately reached for his lower back with his left arm.
A trainer came out to visit Rojas and after a brief discussion he was removed from the game with Tommy Edman taking over mid at-bat. Edman popped up shortly after. The Dodgers released an update shortly after. "Miguel Rojas left tonight's game with low back pain," the team wrote on X.
Latest Update on Miguel Rojas
During the broadcast, Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic reported that Rojas originally suffered the setback while fielding a ground ball back in the 5th inning.
If Rojas' injury is serious enough to keep him out for the remainder of the NLDS, the Dodgers would have to replace him on the roster.
That would also keep him out of the NLCS should Los Angeles advance, which would be a huge loss given the postseason experience he brings.

It was his second consecutive start after he got the nod in Ga
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas has exited Game 3 of the National League Division Series in the top of the eighth inning with an injury.
Rojas appeared to tweak his lower back on a swing and is now out of the game. He initially tweaked his back on a defensive play earlier in the game.
He was replaced by Tommy Edman, who popped out on the first pitch he saw.
Rojas drew the start with the left-handed Chris Sale on the mound. It was his second consecutive start after he got the nod in Game 2 with the lefty Ray Kerr starting.
After going 1-for-1 against Kerr before being replaced by Max Muncy, Rojas was 0-for-3 on Tuesday.
What is Miguel Rojas' Injury?
The Dodgers announced Rojas exited the game with low back pain.
Is Miguel Rojas Retiring After This Season?
Rojas is in the midst of what's expected to be his final season in Major League Baseball. The 37-year-old entered the year saying this would be his last. However, he then left the door open for a potential return in 2027 if the Dodgers won the World Series this year.
Before Tuesday's game, Rojas spoke to reporters and still didn't have a firm answer.
"I'm not thinking about that at all. I'm not thinking about my future or anything," Rojas said. "In regards to my retirement or stepping away from the game, I will never think about stepping away from the game because of my performance or my way to play my game. I think there's other things in life that I'm contemplating about that decision. But if I have to tell you right now, I'm not 100% like [Clayton] Kershaw was last year or others in the past that knew for sure they want to go after this year.
"For me it's more, I would say it's a 40/60 right now that I want to stay in the game and I want to play. But it's not about me. It's about the organization. It's about doing what we're supposed to do to help the team win this year. And then after that we will have conversations."
Rojas, who hit the game-tying home run in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series against the Toronto Blue Jays, had a strong season in 2026, appearing in 105 games and hitting .267 with and OPS of .703. He's still an elite defender in the infield.
Off the field, he's a leader in the Dodgers clubhouse.
Manager Dave Roberts will have an update on his veteran after the game.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dave Roberts Considers Lineup Changes, Won’t Start Josue De Paula
item.dc:creator: Aaron Coloma
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts named potential players who could get a spot in the starting lineup for NLDS Game 3. The Dodgers' offense hasn't been its best through the first two games of the series, relying exclusively on homers to score all seven of their runs so far. Ahead of Tuesday's matchup, Roberts named three players who could insert themselves into the lineup for NLDS Game
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts named potential players who could get a spot in the starting lineup for NLDS Game 3.
The Dodgers' offense hasn't been its best through the first two games of the series, relying exclusively on homers to score all seven of their runs so far. A change of personnel could help the Dodgers string together some hits and bring some more runs across.
Ahead of Tuesday's matchup, Roberts named three players who could insert themselves into the lineup for NLDS Game 3.
"You've got Kiké [Hernandez], you've got [Miguel Rojas], you've got Muncy," Roberts said.
Hernandez provides plenty of positional versatility for the Dodgers, and could stand in at a number of positions if the Dodgers want to approach their matchup against the left-handed Chris Sale with a lineup full of right-handed batters.
The fan favorite's most likely role if he were to start Game 3 would be as the third baseman, keeping left-handed third baseman Max Muncy out of the lineup for a second consecutive game despite hitting homers in each of the first two games of the series, but he could also play either of the corner outfield spots if needed.
Rojas would stand in at second base for Tommy Edman in the most likely case, as Roberts isn't quite ready to move Edman into center to replace Andy Pages despite his rough postseason record.
Who Won't Start for the Dodgers on Tuesday?
In addition to those three players, Roberts revealed Josue De Paula won't have a starting spot against Sale.
"Josue De Paula I don't see being an option," Roberts said.
As a left-handed batter, De Paula's omission from the lineup makes plenty of sense, and he will be available off of the bench for the remainder of the game.
Other than De Paula, Hyeseong Kim and Hunter Feduccia almost certainly won't start, but the rest of the lineup could change as the Dodgers look to find a spark in their offense. With the series tied at one game apiece, the Dodgers need to claim victory in one of their two games in Atlanta to ensure they return home for a game if necessary.
Game 3 could swing momentum in the Dodgers' direction, and they'll do anything to take the lead in the NLDS. Tuesday's game begins at 3:00 p.m. PT.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dave Roberts Ponders Dodger Lineup Tweaks Ahead of Game 3
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb

The Dodgers manager said he is considering lineup tweaks against Chris Sale, including the possibility of moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the order. He also made it clear that Edwin Díaz has worked his way back into serious ninth-inning consideration after his sharp outing in Game 2. With the NLDS tied 1-1, Roberts sounded open to adjusting quickly. Díaz Could Close “I think that we’ve buil
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA, GA — Dave Roberts spent Monday weighing changes on both sides of the ball before Game 3 in Atlanta.
The Dodgers manager said he is considering lineup tweaks against Chris Sale, including the possibility of moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the order. He also made it clear that Edwin Díaz has worked his way back into serious ninth-inning consideration after his sharp outing in Game 2.
With the NLDS tied 1-1, Roberts sounded open to adjusting quickly.
Díaz Could Close
“I think that we’ve built him up, regained the confidence in him and himself,” Roberts said of Díaz. “I think that it’s certainly a viable option for tomorrow night. I feel very confident with him finishing a game.”
Roberts said Díaz’s most recent outing was about as good as he has seen from him.
“That last outing was as good as we’ve seen him throw, and it’s hard to imagine throwing any better,” Roberts said. “He’s put himself in a position to be the closer.
“In October, I don’t pay too much attention to the long sample of a season in a lot of cases, because in October things happen quickly and you’ve got to be willing to read and react.”
Roberts also praised the way Díaz handled a difficult season.
“Character,” he said. “That’s the main thing. When things aren’t going the best and how players respond, that’s telling.
“The way he stayed the course, dealt with the injuries, went to OKC on a longer rehab to work things out and then took on whatever role we had for him says a lot about him.”
Lineup Changes Are on the Table
Roberts also acknowledged that the Dodgers could look different against Sale.
“I am considering it,” he said. “I think that’s a very fair question. I have to be mindful of it being two games, and then within those two games, what have I seen? Are we seeing good at-bats?”
He pointed to Will Smith as someone whose results have not matched the quality of his plate appearances.
“I think Will Smith is taking good at-bats, just missing some pitches, taking good swings, not chasing much,” Roberts said. “Versus other people maybe expanding, trying to do too much.
“Those are things that you’re trying to make bets on. Then you’re looking at tomorrow with Sale, the history, recency, how guys are prepared and will prepare for Sale. So yeah, I’m thinking through that, and there are possible changes.”
Roberts listed Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas and Max Muncy among the options he could work into the lineup.
“At the end of the day, our guys are our guys,” he said. “I can tweak a lineup. I can insert, take out a player or two, but we still have to go out there and play, execute and take good at-bats.”
Moving Ohtani Is Possible
Roberts said he would consider moving Ohtani further down in the order if he believes it helps the team.
“I would,” he said. “I think moving him from one to two, but going further than that, I’m open to it.
“If I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. At the end of the day, every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever is best for the team, he’s all in on. I know that undoubtedly.”
Roberts thinks some of Ohtani’s recent issues have come from trying to do too much.
“I think there’s a little bit of trying to do too much,” he said. “Everything orbits around Shohei in the sense of his talent, and the Braves are going to enter with caution. They’re going to continue to expand as long as we keep giving that to them.
“Until we show some discipline, they’re going to continue to use that playbook.”
He also said Ohtani may be pressing for power.
“Hitting homers, slugging is so much a part of his hallmark in the batter’s box,” Roberts said. “He’s very in tune with what’s being said, what he hasn’t done.
“But that base hit the other way yesterday, that’s production. Against a guy like Chris Sale, that gives you a chance. Trying to chase slug tomorrow night might not be the right plan given the starter.”
Roberts Still Believes in Pages
Andy Pages has also struggled, but Roberts said he plans to keep giving him chances.
“I’m going to continue to give Andy leash,” Roberts said. “I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re going to need him to be an active part of our team.
“This is, for me, given how he has come into the postseason, too small of a sample. He has taken two walks. Tomorrow is not going to be the end-all, be-all because Sale is a tough matchup, but I still want to see good at-bats.”
Roberts believes the main issue is pressing.
“I think there’s trying to do too much,” he said. “When he came back, he was swinging the bat really well, had success, and now I think there’s a little bit of trying too much.”
Freeman Looks Healthier
One hitter Roberts feels especially good about is Freddie Freeman.
“I think he’s gotten into his legs a lot more,” Roberts said. “He’s moving balls in the hitting zone forward. He’s as healthy as he’s been in quite some time. I think the mechanics are sound.”
Roberts credited the five-day break with helping Freeman get his knee into better shape.
“The week off was really crucial for him,” he said. “Being able to manage that with the five days off got him back to health to be able to work through some things without having to perform in a game setting.”
Sale vs. Yamamoto
Roberts expects Sale to attack the Dodgers much the same way he did when Atlanta faced them in August.
“The fastball just sort of bullied us at the top of the zone,” Roberts said. “There was some chase down below, and with the lefties, throwing more two-seamers to keep us honest in and then expand away.”
Still, Roberts believes the Dodgers are in a better offensive place than they were then.
“I do think we are in a different spot,” he said. “The stakes are certainly higher. There is familiarity on both sides. I think we’ll see better at-bats.
“Chris is going to be tough regardless. We know that. We know we’re going to be in for a dogfight, but I just don’t see him bullying us like he did his last start.”
And Roberts feels good about the pitcher the Dodgers will send out against him.
“There should be a lot of talk about Chris Sale, but our guy’s pretty dang good,” Roberts said. “He’s been a very good pitcher in the postseason, so we feel very good about that.
“I think both pitchers are going to pitch well. It’s kind of who grinds out at-bats best.”
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
Move Shohei Ohtani down in the Dodgers’ lineup? Dave Roberts is ‘open’ to it
- Click here to listen to this article
ATLANTA — As the Dodgers mull potential lineup changes for Game 3 of the National League Division Series, manager Dave Roberts said he is “open” to moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the batting order.
In his three seasons with the Dodgers, Ohtani has batted first or second in every game he has started. However, as he has admitted he is trying to “manage” in the aftermath of knee and arm injuries, and as Roberts has acknowledged Ohtani is “not 100%,” the lack of success could compel the manager to replace him at the top of the lineup with a more productive hitter at some point.
“I would,” Roberts said Monday. “I would. I think it’s something that, you know, I think moving him from 1 to 2 — but going further than that? I’m open to it.
“And it’s something that if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. And at the end of the day every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever’s best for the team, he’s all-in on. So I know that undoubtedly.”
It would be strange for the Dodgers to bench Shohei Ohtani, but it’s clear that pretending he’s healthy enough to provide meaningful at-bats isn’t helping.
The Dodgers are batting .215 through the first two games of the NLDS, with the Atlanta Braves scheduled to pitch left-handed ace Chris Sale in Game 3 on Tuesday. If the Dodgers lose, they would need to win back-to-back elimination games to advance beyond this series.
Roberts said the lineup changes he would consider include starting Kiké Hernández and Miguel Rojas, both of whom hit well against left-handers. That could mean infielders Max Muncy (0 for 7 against Sale, with five strikeouts) and Tommy Edman (0 for 11 against Sale) might not start.
Center fielder Andy Pages, who batted so poorly last October he was benched for the final three games of the World Series, is hitless in seven at-bats in this series, with four strikeouts.
“I’m gonna continue to give Andy leash,” Roberts said. “I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re gonna need him to be an active part of our team.
Roberts said he did not envision benching catcher Will Smith, who is 0 for 8 in the series. The Dodgers’ backup catcher, Hunter Feduccia, is a career .205 hitter with no postseason experience.
But, even with the Dodgers’ star-studded lineup, the spotlight shines brightest on Ohtani.
Ohtani has not homered since Aug. 18. He hit .157 between then and the end of the regular season, striking out in 41% of his at-bats. In this series, he has two hits and two strikeouts in eight at-bats, and his inability to refrain from swinging at pitches outside the strike zone has become a glaring weakness.
“He’s not 100%,” Roberts said. “But, at the end of the day, he can still do a better job of staying in the strike zone.”
Ohtani hasn’t given the Braves a reason to challenge him within the strike zone.
“Everything orbits around Shohei, in the sense of his talent,” Roberts said. “And the Braves are going to enter with caution. And, so, knowing that, they’re going to continue to expand as long as we keep giving that to them. So until we show some discipline, they’re going to continue to kind of use that playbook.”

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers consider NLDS Game 3 lineup changes –– with Shohei Ohtani, Kiké Hernández included
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: ATLANTA –– The Dodgers don’t want to overreact to a two-game sample size. But, with elimination all of a sudden just two games away, they don’t want to wait too long to make changes either. That’s what dynamic manager Dave Roberts was grappling with on Monday, as the Dodgers gathered at Truist Park in Atlanta ahead of Game 3 of their National League Division Series against the Braves. A daunting challenge awaits on Tuesday night, when the club will face Braves ace Chris Sale for the first time s
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA –– The Dodgers don’t want to overreact to a two-game sample size.
But, with elimination all of a sudden just two games away, they don’t want to wait too long to make changes either.
That’s what dynamic manager Dave Roberts was grappling with on Monday, as the Dodgers gathered at Truist Park in Atlanta ahead of Game 3 of their National League Division Series against the Braves.
A daunting challenge awaits on Tuesday night, when the club will face Braves ace Chris Sale for the first time since he threw a complete-game shutout against them in August.
Thus, even though the team’s quest for a World Series three-peat just began, potential lineup changes were already under consideration.
And even superstar Shohei Ohtani might not be immune.
“I am considering [changes],” Roberts said. “I think that’s a very fair question.”
That didn’t mean Roberts was ready to commit to any significant alterations ahead of a pivotal Game 3, with the best-of-five series tied one game apiece.
He noted the danger of reading too far into small playoff sample sizes this early in the postseason.
Still, he said there were things he was “thinking through” and “possibly kind of some changes” that could be enacted on Tuesday.
One possibility: Inserting Miguel Rojas and/or Kiké Hernández into lineup, perhaps in place of Max Muncy and/or Tommy Edman, to give the Dodgers extra right-handed bats against a dominant left-hander in Sale.
Another, more notable potential option: Moving Ohtani even further down the order from his current No. 2 spot, after he went just 2-for-8 in the first two games of the NLDS while continuing to battle right arm and left knee injuries.
“[We already moved] him from 1 to 2 –– but going further than that? I’m open to it,” Roberts said. “It’s something that, if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why.”
The explanation, of course, wouldn’t be too complicated.
In Ohtani’s currently diminished physical state, he has simply not been the same presence at the top of the order that the Dodgers have grown accustomed to from the four-time MVP.
“Like we’ve talked about, he’s not 100%,” Roberts said.
But also, “I think there’s a little bit of [him also] trying to do too much,” Roberts added. “I think that’s a piece.”
Indeed, Ohtani has suffered from a futile combination so far in the playoffs, failing to either punish pitches over the plate or keep from chasing out of the strike zone.
“It’s hard to have success when you’re out of the zone,” Roberts said. “So I think that’s the thing, then the question is: How do we get him [attacking pitches back] into it?”
A change of mindset could help, especially against a premium pitcher like Sale (who has held Ohtani to a 3-for-15 mark with five strikeouts and only one double in their career head-to-head matchups).
“Trying to chase slug tomorrow night might not be the right plan, given the starter,” Roberts said.
Instead, Roberts pointed to the opposite-field single Ohtani slapped past a shift for his lone hit in Sunday’s Game 2 loss.
“That at-bat yesterday, the block base hit the other way, that’s something that is production,” Roberts said. “I think that’s something where, against a guy like Chris Sale, it gives you a chance.”
The Dodgers, of course, would love to get more pop from Ohtani, who led the team with eight home runs during last year’s World Series trek. Roberts also knows the slugger “feels the responsibility” to provide such power, which might be contributing to his lack of plate discipline.
Thus, for now, taking the pressure off Ohtani’s shoulders by potentially hitting him lower in the lineup might also prove to be prudent.
“At the end of the day, every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever’s best for the team,” Roberts said. “And he’s all in on [that]. I know that undoubtedly.”
While Roberts will contemplate other changes beyond Ohtani’s spot in the order, there were a few ideas he outright struck down Monday night.
The big one: Removing Andy Pages from the batting order despite his 0-for-7 start in the playoffs –– one that has felt reminiscent of his historic struggles last October, and been further marred by a consequential ABS challenge he missed in Game 1.
While Roberts said he feels Pages has been “trying to do too much” –– downplaying any lingering effects from the fractured hand that sidelined the center fielder for most of September –– he also said he wanted to give the 25-year-old slugger more leash.
“I believe in him,” Roberts said. “And I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re gonna need him to be an active part of our team.”
That was all part of the balance Roberts was trying to strike with his team’s season potentially hanging in the balance. It might still feel early for drastic changes. But one more loss, and the club’s three-peat bid will be on the brink.
“Our guys are our guys,” Roberts said. “Yeah, I can tweak a lineup. I can kind of insert, take out a player or two. But at the end of the day, we still have got to go out there and play and execute and take good at-bats.”

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE -- Los Angeles Dodgers utilitymanKiké Hernandezis expected to be activated in time to make his season debut Monday after recovering from surgery on his left elbow.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said Sunday that Hernández should be available for the start of their home series against the Colorado Rockies.
"There's a different energy with Kiké," Roberts said Sunday. "There's a levity. There's an intensity. There's a good worker in there, a winning player. So I'm looking forward to having that edge."
Hernández, 34, signed a one-year, $4.5 million contract in February that kept him with the Dodgers. He underwent surgery last fall that kept him from playing for Puerto Rico in the World Baseball Classic and delayed the start of his 2026 season.
He hit .214 with a .298 on-base percentage with three RBIs in 12 games while on a rehabilitation assignment with Oklahoma City. He batted .203 with a .255 on-base percentage, 10 homers and 35 RBIs in 92 games with Los Angeles last season.
Hernández often has done his best work in October while helping the Dodgers win World Series in 2020, 2024 and 2025. He has batted .272 with an .826 OPS, 16 homers and 42 RBIs in 103 postseason games.
His return comes while Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy recovers after a 95.5 mph sinker from Milwaukee's Aaron Ashby hit him in the right wrist on Friday. X-rays were negative and the Dodgers expressed optimism that Muncy avoided a major injury.
"We were resolved to not having him available this weekend," Roberts said. "My expectation is that he's getting a little bit better today and maybe swing a bat tomorrow to see. I don't expect him in the lineup tomorrow either."
Muncy is batting .258 with a .363 on-base percentage, .515 slugging percentage, 12 homers and 19 RBIs in 48 games.

item.content:encoded:
El colombiano Didier Fuentes lanzó tres entradas y dos tercios desde el bullpen de los Bravos de Atlanta, ponchó a Shohei Ohtani y ayudó a la victoria por 3-2 sobre los Dodgers de Los Ángeles en el Dodger Stadium. El resultado dejó igualada 1-1 la otra Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional.
Fuentes ingresó en el sexto episodio y permitió un imparable y una carrera limpia, sin otorgar bases por bolas. Realizó 47 lanzamientos, de los cuales 30 fueron strikes, y logró tres ponches durante su primera actuación de postemporada.
El relevista colombiano enfrentó a Ohtani con cuenta completa. Luego de una recta a 162,4 km/h, que fue declarada bola, recurrió a una bola curva 137,3 km/h, para conseguir el tercer strike.
También retiró por la vía del ponche a Will Smith y Freddie Freeman. Fuentes dominó a los primeros 11 bateadores que enfrentó, hasta que Max Muncy conectó un cuadrangular con dos outs en el noveno inning.
Esa es la racha más larga de un relevista de 21 años o menos en un juego de postemporada en la historia de la MLB. Ningún relevista de 21 años o menos ha tenido una racha tan larga en un juego de temporada regular desde Tom Gordon el 12 de abril de 1989, según lo publicado por Opta Stats en su perfil de X.
El único punto negativo de la jornada para el joven beisbolista cafetero fue el jonrón de Muncy impulsó la entrada de Iglesias, quien retiró al único bateador al que se enfrentó para conseguir la victoria. Pero eso no arruinó lo que fue una noche memorable para Fuentes, quien lanzó cuatro rectas a más de 99 mph en la novena entrada.
“Fue muy emotivo y emocionante. Así que le doy gracias a Dios por la ayuda que me ha permitido mantenerme sano y poder competir”, dijo el nacido en Tolú, Sucre, tras su primera gran noche en la liga más importante de béisbol en el mundo.
“¿Tiene 21 o 22 años? Está haciendo eso a esa edad. Es increíble, sobre todo lanzar a 100 millas por hora. Se enfrenta a situaciones de alto nivel y las supera. Fue realmente impresionante” dijo Kerr, el lanzador principal de los Bravos de Atlanta, sobre Fuentes.
Mientras que Matt Olson, primera base de los Bravos, se refirió a la potencia en el brazo que tiene el colombiano: “No podía creer que volviera a lanzar en la novena entrada, pero lo hizo y seguía lanzando a 100 millas por hora. Eso fue impresionante.”
“Después de su tercera entrada, miré a nuestro entrenador de lanzadores y le dije: ‘Veamos cómo se siente’”, dijo Weiss. “Si se siente bien, quiero que vuelva a lanzar. No quería cambiar algo que funcionaba bien. Estaba lanzando muy bien”, declaró el manager del equipo.
Los Bravos habían abierto el marcador con un sencillo productor de Mauricio Dubón en el primer episodio. Freeman igualó para los Dodgers con un jonrón solitario en el cuarto, pero Atlanta volvió a tomar la ventaja en el quinto mediante una jugada que permitió anotar a Michael Harris II.
Harris amplió el marcador en el séptimo con un doblete productor que llevó a Matt Olson al plato. Fuentes se anotó su primer hold, la estadística asignada a un relevista que preserva una ventaja en una situación comprometida. La serie se trasladará a Atlanta para el tercer juego, programado para el martes a las 5:00 p. m., hora de Colombia.
En las Series Divisionales con el formato actual 2-2-1, los equipos que consiguen dividir victorias como visitantes antes de regresar a casa para los Juegos 3 y 4 han ganado la serie 30 de 49 veces (61%).

item.title: [heavy.com] Dodgers’ Mookie Betts Makes Feelings Clear After Loss to Braves
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are heading to Atlanta with their home-field advantage gone. A 3-2 loss in Game 2 of the National League Division Series on Sunday night evened the series at one game apiece and handed the Braves exactly the split they were looking for. The Dodgers failed to deliver a single hit in eight chances with runners in scoring position over the two home games. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are heading to Atlanta with their home-field advantage gone. A 3-2 loss in Game 2 of the National League Division Series on Sunday night evened the series at one game apiece and handed the Braves exactly the split they were looking for.
The Dodgers failed to deliver a single hit in eight chances with runners in scoring position over the two home games. The offense that was supposed to carry them through October has yet to find a consistent rhythm.
After the loss, one of the team’s veteran leaders offered a straightforward assessment of where things stand.
Betts Sets the Tone for Atlanta
Mookie Betts did not sugarcoat the challenge but refused to frame the situation as a crisis.
“It’s just not gonna be easy,” Betts said. “But I mean we knew that from the beginning… We know it’s gonna be a tough matchup, no matter who’s on the mound.”
The comment reflected the mentality of a player who has been through deep October runs before. Betts helped the Dodgers win titles in 2024 and 2025. He knows what the grind looks like, and he knows that a tied series heading into a road game is far from a death sentence.
Still, there was no dodging what happened Sunday. The Dodgers had their best opportunity in the fifth inning with two runners on and nobody out but came away empty. Six different Braves relievers held the lineup in check for the majority of the night.
Betts’ Game 2 Showed the Problem
Betts finished 0-for-2 with a pair of walks in Game 2. He reached base, drew pitches, and did his part to set the table from the leadoff spot. The production behind him did not follow.
The Dodgers collected just four hits beyond Freddie Freeman‘s game-tying home run in the fourth. Max Muncy added a solo shot in the ninth to pull within a run, but by then the damage had been done.
Through two games, the pattern is clear. When the lineup cannot string hits together, it relies on the long ball. That approach has a ceiling, and the Dodgers hit it Sunday.
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 03: Mookie Betts #50 of the Los Angeles Dodgers throws to first base during the seventh inning against the Atlanta Braves in game one of the National League Division Series at Dodger Stadium on October 03, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images)
Final Word for the Dodgers
Chris Sale is waiting in Atlanta. The Braves ace held the Dodgers scoreless when the two teams met in the regular season and will have the benefit of additional rest heading into Game 3 on Tuesday.
Betts’ message was simple. This was never going to be easy. The series is tied, the road gets harder, and the Dodgers need their lineup to find a way beyond home runs.
Two games in, that is the one thing they have not figured out.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers lost to the Atlanta Braves, 3-2, on Sunday as the National League Division Series evened out to one game apiece. With the best-of-five series now heading back to Atlanta, the two-time defending champions are in a much more troublesome spot than expected.
Left-hander Blake Snell was far from his best on Sunday as he struck out five across 3.2 innings of work (90 pitches) with an earned run and five walks. Snell, Kris Bubic and Edgardo Henriquez all allowed an earned run while the four remaining relievers were hitless in their respective outings.
Offensively, Freddie Freeman tied things up in the fourth inning with a solo home run, just his second since the All-Star break. When the Dodgers were down to their final out, Max Muncy slugged a solo home run — but it was too little too late for LA.
The Dodgers also officially announced that the starter for Game 3 of the NLDS will be the ace: Right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto. The reigning World Series MVP had a 2.16 ERA in his last five regular season starts and will now make his 2026 postseason debut.
Yamamoto will face off against southpaw Chris Sale for the Braves, who is working with a 2.16 ERA across 27 starts this season. So far in the postseason, Sale struck out nine across 6.1 innings in Atlanta's first wild-card game, and on one day of rest, closed out Game 3 of the wild-card round with three strikeouts across the game's final four outs.
Finally, manager Dave Roberts made a bold prediction regarding right fielder Kyle Tucker following his abysmal regular season to kick off the Dodgers chapter of his career. Tucker was hitting just .228 with 11 home runs going into September before he appeared to start to turn things around
“It’s been fun to watch Kyle build some confidence," Roberts said before the NLDS. "You can see him just freed up a little bit. He’s been working hard this whole year, and he’s been in it. And I give him a lot of credit for continuing to persevere and [I] expect the best of him to be at the end of the season.”

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Max Muncy's Focused on What Dodgers Can Control until NLDS
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers have spent much of 2026 with history hanging over them, but Max Muncy says the players have little interest in making that history their daily focus. His message throughout the session was
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers have spent much of 2026 with history hanging over them, but Max Muncy says the players have little interest in making that history their daily focus.
As the Dodgers prepare for another postseason run, Muncy spoke with reporters Tuesday about the chance to win a third straight World Series, how the club plans to handle its five-day bye, possible Division Series opponents and what years of October baseball have taught this group. His message throughout the session was simple. The Dodgers know what lies ahead, and they have learned a few things about how to get ready for it.
Keeping the Three-Peat Talk in the Background
The Dodgers enter October with a chance to accomplish something baseball has not seen in decades, but Muncy said the players have enough pressure simply trying to win another championship.
“Obviously it’s there, but it’s not something that we’re really focused on. We’re trying to focus on ourselves, getting ready this week, paying attention to whoever we might be playing and just trying to get ready for a postseason series the same way we’ve always gotten ready for it.
“We don’t need to be adding any extra pressure onto ourselves. We’ve been saying that for a long time. When you talk about three-peating, you’re putting that extra pressure that doesn’t need to be there. Winning the World Series is already hard enough as it is. So for us, we’re just trying to focus on what we have ahead of us without the added noise to it.”
Been There, Done That
That work starts during the five-day break before the Division Series. The Dodgers have been through the bye before, and Muncy said the club learned an important lesson in 2024 about keeping players around one another and maintaining a postseason mindset.
“One of the formulas that clearly worked for us was not giving guys too much time. You’ve earned the bye and you should take that time to rest and recover, but you don’t want to give guys too much time to be at home and get that taste of what it might be like.
“That really worked for us back in 2024. You get guys here to the field. You’re not forcing anyone to do anything, but you’re making all the guys hang out together for extended periods of time when they could be at home enjoying family time, which is great for everybody, but not when you know what’s coming for us ahead.
“You’re going to be facing a team that’s already been through the fire. They’ve already been through the emotions. They’ve already been through the roller coaster, which is the postseason. It’s hard to go from being in an at-home setting to trying to find a way to flip the switch.
“The best way for us to do that was to get everyone together, keep them at the field and find a way to not let that switch ever be flipped off. That was something that I thought we did a really good job of in ’24, and we’re going to try to do it again this year.”
Whoever Shows Up, Shows Up
The Dodgers will spend the week watching the Wild Card round and learning who comes next. Muncy said the club will prepare for the possible opponents while keeping most of its attention on its own work.
“We have to focus on ourselves, but we also have to focus on which team we might be playing. So we’re obviously very clearly paying attention to that. Either team, it doesn’t really matter. You’re going to have to play nothing but good teams from here on out.
No Bad Teams in the Field
“It’s the postseason. You don’t make it in as a bad team. Any team can go out there and beat you. For us, you have to focus on the things that you need to be doing day in and day out. We have five days to get ourselves ready for a game, and whoever we play is whoever we play.
“I know you guys have heard me say it a bunch. You don’t necessarily play the other team as much as you play yourself. Obviously, there’s a starting pitcher on the other side that you have to pay attention to and focus on, but if you’re not doing the things that you need to do to get ready, it doesn’t matter who you’re going to play. You’re probably not going to go out there and have a good time.”
Muncy has now been through enough Octobers to know how little the regular season can tell anyone about what comes next.
“Every team has the ability to (win). That’s the one thing that I’ve noticed over the years. It all comes down to who’s going to play good baseball, who gets hot, who’s going to have the pitching, who’s going to get one hitter that gets really, really hot.
“There’s not really any proper way to guess it. Obviously when you look on paper, there are certain teams you think are better than others, but you kind of throw that all out the window when it comes to the postseason. Any team can go out there and win, and that’s why it’s such a fun time to play in October.”
Momentum, Matchups and October Baseball
The Dodgers finished the regular season with the offense swinging the bats well, and Muncy hopes some of that carries into the Division Series.
“You certainly hope so. You hope that there’s a little bit of momentum there. I always hate when people say ‘lesser opponents.’ This is the big leagues. These are the best players in the world. I know there are teams that don’t have as good records as others, but that doesn’t mean that they’re bad players.
“These are all still really, really good players. We’re still facing really, really good pitching. For us, we throw those comments kind of out the window because it just doesn’t matter. You’re still facing big league pitching. It’s still really tough to go out there and do.
“For us to have a really good month and to get the momentum going, obviously you hope that carries over and you can pick up where you left off.”
The Dodgers also had their share of struggles against playoff-bound clubs during the season. Muncy pointed to past Octobers as proof that head-to-head records carry little weight once a postseason series starts.
“How many years have we seen it? In ’22, we beat the Padres something like 16 times in the regular season and then they beat us in the postseason. It just doesn’t matter.
“You see it every single year where there’s a team that really struggled against another team and then they go out there and kind of just take it to them in the postseason. I know there are things you look at on paper where you say this is a good matchup, but in October it really doesn’t matter.”
The One Thing the Dodgers Cannot Recreate
The Dodgers will hold workouts, live at-bats and simulated games during the bye. Muncy believes those can help hitters and pitchers maintain their timing. The tougher part is recreating what it feels like when a real October game begins.
“I think the hardest thing to replicate is the emotion of it. You can do live at-bats, you can do sim games, you can do any number of things to stay sharp and have your timing still there in terms of a baseball sense.
“It’s not even like a rehab assignment where you go down and play games and then come back up. There’s just no way of replicating the emotion that goes into playing a postseason game.
“The emotion, the stress, the ups and downs throughout the course of a game, you just can’t get that any other way other than playing a game. To me, that’s always going to be the hardest thing to replicate.”
Muncy also sounded confident in the Dodgers’ defense despite some uneven stretches during the regular season.
“I think we’re a good defensive team. Throughout the course of the season you have those ups and downs, but for the majority of the season, I would say we were a very good defensive team.
“That’s where I would lay my hat. We’re going to make the plays come October and we’re going to do what we need to do. We have the experience to do what we need to do. Everything that we do from a preparation standpoint, I always feel like that helps us out, and I think that’s going to be key for us again.”

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The potential road to history for the Los Angeles Dodgers begins with a reunion as the National League Division Series starts Saturday afternoon with a visit from the Atlanta Braves.
Freddie Freeman has been a major postseason contributor during the Dodgers’ consecutive World Series titles, and the veteran will be in the heart of the order again in a matchup against his former team.
Freeman also was invaluable in the 2021 World Series when the Braves won their most recent title. Freeman joined the Dodgers as a free agent in 2022 after Atlanta moved on to Matt Olson as their first baseman.
While Freeman has won three rings in five seasons, the Dodgers are trying to become the first National League club to win championships in three consecutive years. Only two American League franchises have ever done it: the New York Yankees and Oakland Athletics.
The Yankees were the last to accomplish the feat when they won championships in 1998, 1999 and 2000.
“We don’t need to be adding any extra pressure onto ourselves,” Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy said. “We’ve been saying that for a long time. When you talk about three-peating, you’re putting that extra pressure on it that doesn’t need to be there. Winning a World Series is already hard enough as it is.”
After returning from a biceps injury during the final week of the regular season, Shohei Ohtani will be back atop the Los Angeles order when the club’s postseason run begins.
Left-hander Tarik Skubal was named the Dodgers’ Game 1 starter over right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Skubal arrived just before the trade deadline in a deal with the Detroit Tigers and went 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA in 10 starts for his new club.
Skubal is 0-1 with a 4.91 ERA in two career starts against Atlanta, including an outing in April when he gave up two runs over seven innings in a no-decision.
The Braves opened their postseason by getting past the Philadelphia Phillies in the wild-card round. Atlanta won a winner-take-all Game 3 on Thursday behind a three-run home run from Michael Harris II and a dominating day on the mound. Six pitchers kept Philadelphia in check, including staff ace Chris Sale, who recorded the final four outs.
The Braves face the Dodgers after going 5-1 against them in the regular season, including a three-game home sweep in late August.
“Everyone knows the Dodgers have a juggernaut, but we played well against them this year,” Atlanta manager Walt Weiss said. “I know that doesn’t carry a whole lot of stock. Once the playoffs begin, everybody starts at zero. The Dodgers are healthier now than they were when we saw them.”
Weiss has yet to name his Game 1 starter, with a left-handed opener a possibility to line up against early left-handed bats like Ohtani and Freeman.
The Braves will continue to be without a pair of starters in right-hander Bryce Elder (knee) and left-hander Martin Perez (back).
Like Freeman before him, Olson has emerged as a Braves leader, along with Ronald Acuna Jr. Olson hit a team-best 41 home runs in the regular season and added another in the wild-card round. Harris hit 26 home runs in the regular season and Acuna added 20 homers and 21 steals.
“I think it’s just kind of going out there and playing our game and knowing that … we can compete with them and beat them,” said Braves catcher Drake Baldwin, an All-Star and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year who contributed 25 home runs.
–Doug Padilla, Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — With the end of the regular season on Sunday, the statisticians can finally put down their pencils. We had a near miss for the triple crown in the American League (Yordan Alvarez) and a pitcher with a sub-2.00 ERA in the National League (Jacob Misiorowski). And though no Dodgers were at the top of any statistically categories this year, there were plenty featured in the NL Top Ten. Let’s do a quick end-of-season rundown, shall we?
The plan for two-way dominance Cy Young/MVP consideration sort of flamed out before the All-Star break, and Shohei was struggling to find his footing at the plate in the aftermath of a couple of injuries (most notably his right knee). However, even a diminished Ohtani is among the league’s elite and Shohei did enough in the first half of the season to lock down some Top-Ten finishes. He was tied for ninth in home runs with 30, tied for tenth in walks with 81, and 19th in batting average with .275. His other numbers were also top-ten-worthy: he finished sixth in the NL in On-Base Percentage with .377 and fifth in slugging percentage with .512. And, finally, his OPS of .889 was more than 100 lower than last year, but still third in the league behind Chicago’s Pete Crow-Armstrong and the Nationals’ James Wood.
It was good year. But considering the wow factor of the first two years, a bit of a disappointment. Hopefully, he can get right in time to do damage like the old Shohei in the playoffs.
Despite his mighty struggles in September, Freddie turned in another strong campaign in 2026. Although his power number were down considerably, he still found his way on base at a clip not often seen in the modern game. Though his .288 batting average represented a low in Freddie’s Dodger years, it was still good enough for tenth place in the league. And, his 167 hits put him in eighth place in that category.
For those of you keeping track, he now stands at 2,598 hits in his career, 402 shy of the 3,000 mark that he’s had on his mind for a while. He’ll probably need three more years in the big league to reach that plateau, so that means the Dodgers would have to re-sign him after his current contract expires at the end of next year. Will that happen? It should, but I don’t know if Andrew Friedman wants to be sentimental about such things.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto was the only Dodger pitcher who logged enough innings to qualify for postseason awards, and he’s sure to get at least a sniff or two in the Cy Young voting. His year was probably his best yet: Fifth in wins (14), 3rd in ERA (2.53), 4th in innings pitched (185), 10th in strikeouts (182), 2nd in WHIP, and 2nd in Average Against (.182). Of course, all the hardwares going to the Miz this year, but Yamamoto’s steadiness is something to behold even if he doesn’t light up the radar gun on every pitch.
After a horrible year in 2025, no one was quite sure what to expect from Tanner Scott in 2026, and when Edwin Diaz went out with injury, there were more than a few Dodger fans who dreaded the thought of last year’s goat closing out games. However, Scott proved more than up to the task, converting 25 of 29 save opportunities, which put him in sixth place in the NL leader board. It will be interesting to see what happens as a resurgent Edwin Diaz seems to be ready for a return to the closer’s role.
Honorable mention….
Though they didn’t make any top tens, we should give it for Max Muncy, who made the All-Star team and finished 13th in the league in OPS and tied for 14th in the NL for homers. A really solid season from Max. Alex Vesia finished 7th in the league in appearances, and had an impact on more games than you might think. And, though they’re nowhere on the leaderboard, the strong finishes for Mookie Betts, Teoscar Hernandez, and Kyle Tucker gives one hope for the postseason.
What about the team?
Since the Dodgers won the second most games in baseball, it only figures that they’d have a lot of nice numbers at the end of the year. On the hitting side, they finished fourth in home runs (204), fourth in RBI (756), 3rd in batting average (.257), second in slugging percentage (.424), and second in OPS (.762).
On the pitching side, they finished second in team ERA (3.55), 3rd in strikeouts (1,521), first in WHIP (1.18), and first in average against (.218). When you isolate the starters, the numbers are even better: first place in ERA, WHIP, and average against, and second in strikeouts.
The bullpen was good, but closer to the middle of the pack in the NL: fourth in ERA, fourth in saves, and fourth in WHIP. One stat that may work in the pen’s favor though: they finished 14th out of 15 NL teams in bullpen innings pitched. That means that other pens (save the Phillies) have been taxed more than the Dodgers. That could make a difference the deeper we go into October.
Conclusion
The numbers show kind of how 2026 felt: it was a good year, but not a dominant year. Many players, while still contributing, were down from their historical norms. And if the past is prologue, look for a lot of low-scoring games this October. Games that might be decided by one swing of the bat or one shut-down inning.
In the meantime, we wait. We watch and we wait.
See you Saturday!
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
Now that the 2026 MLB regular season is done, Sony made one last ratings tweak for many of the players across the league on October 2. The October MLB The Show 26 ratings update saw Mookie Betts & Cade Smith rise to join the other Diamonds in the game.
The notable changes
Mookie Betts is back as a Diamond in MLB The Show 26. He and Cade Smith were the only two to move to Diamond status on October 2. Betts moved to 85 OVR after a strong final few weeks. Over his last 14 games, Betts slashed .316/.418/.632 with four home runs and 10 extra-base hits.
Smith, meanwhile, notched 41 saves and struck out 107 batters over 74 innings this season for the Guardians.
Fernando Tatis Jr. moved up three points between the last update and now. Tatis Jr., before the start of the playoffs, hit five home runs and nine extra-base hits in the last 15 games of the regular season for San Diego.
Elly De La Cruz, who had eight extra-base hits in the final two weeks, moved to 87 OVR, a +2 OVR increase. He moved there, along with NL Wild Card hero Michael Harris II.
As for who went down, Yandy Diaz and Jacob deGrom were both downgraded from Diamond status.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers se lo toman con calma: van por el histórico “three-peat” en la MLB
Los Ángeles busca convertirse en el primer equipo desde los Yankees de 1998-2000 en ganar tres Series Mundiales consecutivas.
PUBLICIDAD
Los Ángeles. Freddie Freeman y Emmet Sheehan bostezaron. El mánager Dave Roberts usó pantalones cortos para la práctica de bateo.
Los Dodgers de Los Ángeles se lo toman con calma mientras se encaminan a una postemporada potencialmente histórica.
Intentan convertirse en el primer equipo desde los Yankees de Nueva York de 1998-2000 en ganar tres Series Mundiales consecutivas. Serían el primer club de la Liga Nacional en lograrlo.
Y dejarían las expectativas altísimas para todos los demás.
“No es algo en lo que realmente estemos enfocados. Cuando hablas de ganar tres seguidas, le estás poniendo esa presión extra que no tiene por qué estar ahí“, comentó el antesalista Max Muncy. ”Ganar una Serie Mundial ya es lo suficientemente difícil”.
Los Dodgers disputaron un juego simulado el jueves, mientras se proyectaba el duelo decisivo de la serie de comodines de la Liga Nacional entre Filadelfia y Atlanta en las pantallas de video del estadio. Los Bravos vencieron a los Filis por 6-2 y jugarán en Los Ángeles el primer duelo de la serie divisional de la Liga Nacional, al mejor en un máximo de cinco encuentros, el sábado, cuando se pronostica que la temperatura alcance los 100 grados Fahrenheit (38 Celsius) para el juego diurno.
“Te enfrentas a un equipo que ya pasó por el fuego y ya vivió la emoción”, comentó Muncy.
Los Dodgers han pasado la semana de descanso recuperándose, mientras alternaban práctica de bateo en vivo y en la jaula con juegos simulados en un estadio mayormente silencioso. Aparte de las canciones de entrada al plato, los únicos sonidos eran el chasquido del bate, los gritos de los jugadores desde las bancas y los jardineros avisando a sus compañeros que ellos se encargarían de un elevado.
Freeman aprovechó el tiempo para concentrarse en ajustar la mecánica de su swing mientras lidiaba una molestia en la rodilla derecha. El plan del primera base de 37 años incluía hacer 400 swings “con la esperanza de quitarme los malos hábitos”, explicó.
En el inicio del juego simulado del jueves, conectó un doble ante Tyler Glasnow.
“De verdad me siento bien físicamente ahora mismo y depende de mí resolver la mecánica del swing”, comentó. ”No tengo dolor en la rodilla en este momento”.
Shohei Ohtani, cuatro veces nombrado el Jugador Más Valioso, ha lidiado durante semanas con molestias persistentes en el bíceps derecho y la rodilla izquierda. La rodilla lo frenó para lanzar y el brazo lo llevó recientemente a la lista de lesionados por primera vez con los Dodgers.
Regresó a tiempo para jugar en cinco partidos al final de la temporada.
Aún está por verse qué versión de Ohtani tendrán los Dodgers en la serie divisional de la Liga Nacional. Sin embargo, Roberts dijo que “se siente muy bien físicamente. Sus swings, en general, están en un gran punto”.
La alineación de jugadores de posición de los Dodgers es la de mayor edad en las Grandes Ligas, encabezada por el infielder venezolano Miguel Rojas, de 37 años, Freeman y Muncy, de 35. Ohtani tiene 32. El relevista Blake Treinen tiene 38, pero se perderá la postemporada tras lesionarse el fin de semana pasado.
“Creo que la experiencia va a ser enorme. Sabemos lo que se necesita”, aseveró Freeman
Al mismo tiempo, advirtió que los Dodgers no deben adelantarse.
“Si en este momento piensas en el panorama general, vas a perder de vista las cosas”.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dodgers Notes: Glasnow's Role, Freeman's Knee & More
item.dc:creator: Cody Snavely
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA—The start of the 2026 National League Division Series is just two days away, and the Dodgers have spent the last couple of days getting their final work in before October officially begins. With Los Angeles enjoying the first-round bye, the extra time has allowed the team to rest, prepare, and get healthy while also giving us plenty to talk about from workouts. From Tyler Glasnow’s potential role and Freddie Freeman’s knee to the Dodgers patiently waiting to find out who they’ll
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA—The start of the 2026 National League Division Series is just two days away, and the Dodgers have spent the last couple of days getting their final work in before October officially begins.
With Los Angeles enjoying the first-round bye, the extra time has allowed the team to rest, prepare, and get healthy while also giving us plenty to talk about from workouts. From Tyler Glasnow’s potential role and Freddie Freeman’s knee to the Dodgers patiently waiting to find out who they’ll face in the NLDS, several interesting developments have emerged around camp.
So, with the weekend quickly approaching, here’s the latest from Dodgers camp as Los Angeles gets ready to begin its three-peat chase.
Tyler Glasnow Unlikely to Repeat His Bullpen Role From Last October for NLDS
While the Dodgers await the outcome of today’s final Wild Card game between the Phillies and Braves, they have begun laying the groundwork for their pitching staff ahead of Saturday’s NLDS opener.
While Dodgers manager Dave Roberts did not confirm the team’s starting rotation order for the series, he did allude to the fact that right-hander Tyler Glasnow likely won’t be used in relief, as he was during last NLDS against the Phillies.
A big reason is the scheduling of this year’s series compared to last season, with Games One and Two on back-to-back days rather than an odd day off between them.
“He’s one of four (starting pitchers),” Roberts began. “I think it’s a little different with the layout of the games in the DS, not playing in the Wild Card also. Could he factor in one of the first three games? Possibly.
“I would say most likely Game Four. I don’t see him out of the bullpen early. We’re going to talk through that in the next couple of days here.”
That makes a repeat of last year’s strategy unlikely. The Dodgers could still turn to Glasnow out of the bullpen later in the postseason if the situation calls for it, particularly in an elimination game, but for now, it appears his focus will remain on starting.
Still, Glasnow was elite in that role last season, tossing 1.2 scoreless innings between Games One and Two at Citizena Bank Park and proceeded to toss six more shutout innings in the Dodgers’ extra-inning walk-off victory in Game Four.
Freeman Says His Knee Is Feeling Good as He Looks to Reset Before the NLDS
Having the first-round bye for the Dodgers was seen as essential by many members of the organization and the media. Still, none preached for it more than Dodgers veteran first baseman Freddie Freeman, and that makes sense given his late-season struggles and apparent knee injury.
Freddie Freeman’s knee appears to be in a much better spot heading into the Dodgers’ NLDS matchup, giving him five full days during the postseason bye to focus on getting his swing back on track.
Freeman was held out of the lineup for multiple games late in the regular season, but the Dodgers never placed him on the injured list. While the extra rest helped his knee, his offensive struggles continued, as he hit just .226/.300/.278 over his final 30 games and .184 with a .513 OPS in September.
Still, Freeman isn’t using the knee as an excuse.
“My body feels good. I think that’s the main thing,” Freeman said Tuesday. “I feel like it’s in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing.”
Freeman acknowledged the knee may have contributed to some bad habits at the plate, but ultimately blamed himself.
“I’ll never blame anything physical-wise for why I didn’t play well,” Freeman said. “I just didn’t play well the last couple of months of the season.”
Now, Freeman sees the five-day break as a valuable opportunity to reset without the pressure of immediately taking his work into a game.
“My knee’s in a good spot now, that’s why the bye week is huge,” Freeman said. “Personally, it’s huge for me that I’ve got five days to really work on the mechanics of my swing.”
With live at-bats against Dodgers pitchers planned during the break, Freeman will have plenty of time to iron out those mechanical issues before the NLDS begins Saturday.
Dodgers Keeping Three-Peat Talk in the Background, Focused on One Game at a Time
All that talk around Major League Baseball and throughout Los Angeles will be whether the back-to-back champion Dodgers can become the first National League team to three-peat.
And while that will be a major storyline following the Dodgers this October for every series they’re in, that is not the focus of the players and coaches in the clubhouse.
The three-peat has been on the Dodgers’ minds since last year’s World Series parade, but with the NLDS just days away, the players aren’t interested in adding that pressure to an already difficult task.
Max Muncy acknowledged the goal is there, but said the Dodgers are focused on preparing for their next series rather than thinking about the bigger picture.
“I mean, obviously it’s there, but it’s not something that we’re really focused on,” Muncy said. “We don’t need to be adding any extra pressure onto ourselves. When you talk about three-peating, you’re putting that extra pressure that doesn’t need to be there. Winning the World Series is already hard enough as it is.”
Freddie Freeman has a similar mindset, making it clear his attention is on the NLDS and nothing beyond it.
“Personally, I’m not thinking about three-peat,” Freeman said. “I’m thinking about the NLDS and whoever we play, and getting ready for that. I think if you think big picture in this moment, you’re going to lose sight of some things.”
Dave Roberts echoed his players, saying the Dodgers understand what’s at stake without needing to discuss it constantly.
“Our guys understand what’s at stake,” Roberts said. “I think for me, it’s balancing the importance, the opportunity that we have. Versus trying to add more pressure than there already is.”
The Dodgers know they have a chance to make history, but for now, the message throughout the clubhouse is simple: focus on the next series, not the three-peat.
Dodgers’ NLDS Opponent Still Up in the Air After Phillies-Braves Split
Later today, the Dodgers will finally know who they’ll face in the best-of-five NLDS that kicks off Saturday at Dodger Stadium, whether it’s the Phillies or Braves.
The Phillies rallied for a 4-3, 10-inning win over the Braves, tying the Wild Card Series and forcing a winner-take-all Game Three Thursday. That means the Dodgers’ eventual NLDS opponent will have to play three games in three days just to reach Los Angeles.
That’s a significant advantage for the Dodgers.
While Philadelphia and Atlanta are burning through their pitching staffs, Los Angeles is resting, preparing, and lining up its rotation. Whoever survives Thursday will arrive in Los Angeles having already played three high-pressure postseason games while the Dodgers have been sitting at home.
Philadelphia, in particular, had to dig deep Wednesday. Cristopher Sánchez threw 116 pitches over 6⅔ innings, while Andrew Painter recorded the final nine outs. If the Phillies advance, Zack Wheeler would presumably start Game Three, potentially affecting his availability for the NLDS opener.
That could be especially important considering Wheeler, Sánchez and Jesús Luzardo give Philadelphia one of the more formidable rotations in the postseason.
But Atlanta won’t escape unscathed either. Chris Sale already threw six innings in Game One, while Tyler Mahle delivered seven strong innings Wednesday. Both teams have used key starters and relievers, with one more game to go.
The Dodgers don’t have to win a Wild Card game. They don’t even have to play one. Their opponent does.
So while Los Angeles waits to find out whether it will be Philadelphia or Atlanta, it’s also watching its eventual opponent spend three games, three days, and a whole lot of pitching just to earn the right to come to Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers’ NLDS opponent remains up in the air. The advantage of making that team play all three games, however, is already locked in.

item.dc:creator: Andy Lane Chapman
item.description: As the Los Angeles Dodgers await the outcome of the final game between the Philadelphia Philles and Atlanta Braves to see who they will face in the NLDS, the team is busy working on keeping their bats and arms fresh and ready for the road to a three-peat that lies ahead. As Bill Plunkett of the OC Register notes, the last two championship wins were won mainly on the backs of the pitchers – the bullpen in 2024, and key starters in 2025. Could this finally be the year that the Dodgers win it by ha
item.content:encoded:
As the Los Angeles Dodgers await the outcome of the final game between the Philadelphia Philles and Atlanta Braves to see who they will face in the NLDS, the team is busy working on keeping their bats and arms fresh and ready for the road to a three-peat that lies ahead.
As Bill Plunkett of the OC Register notes, the last two championship wins were won mainly on the backs of the pitchers – the bullpen in 2024, and key starters in 2025. Could this finally be the year that the Dodgers win it by having their offense outslug the other teams?
"It would be nice to slug our way to a World Series one of these years," third baseman Max Muncy joked on the eve of another postseason run. "We can't keep letting the pitchers take all the credit, right?"
The offense has looked better in the month of September, and they hope to continue that and have those that weren't hitting join those that are. Plunkett has more thoughts from the players on how they're looking to perform in the playoffs here.
As Bill Shakin of the L.A. Times notes, the last two World Series runs have had signature moments from Freddie Freeman, and ponders if this playoff run will have the same.
"My body feels good," Freeman said. "I think that's the main thing. I feel like it's in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing and everything that's been going on the last couple months."
Shakin goes on to cover Freeman's lackluster second half, and has more quotes from the man himself here.
As the team moves into its newest playoff era, one player is contemplating the end of his own. Miguel Rojas announced at the beginning of the season that he would be retiring at the end of this season. Now, he's not quite so sure. Maddie Chen of the L.A.Times talks about how Rojas is facing the possible end of his career.
"From this moment on, it will be kind of like a day-to-day thing," he said. "And you might get to know that I'm stepping away from the game in an Instagram post, or from me just saying goodbye on a video. I don't know. I don't know how it's going to be, but at this moment, I'm not 100% [certain]."

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula, bench shuffle
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA. One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered. Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA.
One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered.
Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula called upon
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
For some reason, the Dodgers decided to carry three catchers on their Wild Card and NLDS rosters last year — Smith, Dalton Rushing, and Ben Rortvedt — but adjusted ahead of the NLCS by shedding Rushing, who received just one at-bat in the NLDS but otherwise rode the bench.
Rortvedt didn't get a start or even substitution after Game 2 of the NLDS with Smith slowly coming back from injury at the beginning of the postseason. Feduccia figures to play a similar break-glass-in-case-of-emergency role. As a lefty, he could get a start and then an early pull depending on matchups but, barring disaster, it's mostly going to be Smith's show.
Designated hitters (2): Shohei Ohtani, Josue De Paula
The Dodgers clearly want to find a way to bring De Paula with them in October, even if only as a lingering threat on their bench. They're reportedly not entertaining putting him in the outfield at all, and it's not hard to see why. Even if they're confident they'll be able to fix his defense in time, they can't afford any leakage in the postseason.
Ohtani is still shaking off the cobwebs from his 15-day IL stint. He picked up a few hits with promising exit velocity in his return against the San Diego Padres and later against the San Francisco Giants, but there are still question marks around what version of him we might see this postseason.
Infielders (6): Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman, Max Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández
A notable exclusion here is Hyeseong Kim. Although he's in the running to get a spot on the bench and exclusively come into games to pinch-run or for reassurances on defense, there's still a chance he doesn't make the roster if the Dodgers are set on carrying 13 pitchers. Edman and Hernández, though lacking the same speed as Kim, can still offer the same defensive versatility.
Outfielders (3): Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández
Pages might've found himself in the same boat as Ohtani, but he announced his return to the Dodgers after a month-long IL stint in a big way, hitting .333 with a 1.180 OPS, two homers, and five RBI against the Padres and Giants. No doubt Dave Roberts and Andrew Friedman breathed a massive sigh of relief.
Alex Call will be the odd man out. He was on all four of LA's playoff rosters last year and received sporadic appearances throughout the month, but that was when Michael Conforto was still on the payroll. Tucker and Hernández have certainly had their ups-and-downs this season, but the Dodgers would never seriously consider leaving them out.
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow
There's not much to say about what's probably the best rotation going into the postseason. Snell and Glasnow have both battled injury this season but came back when the Dodgers needed them most. It might be too much to ask that any of Yamamoto, Snell, or Glasnow replicate their dominance from last year, but they'll certainly try.
Relievers: (9): Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski, Edwin Díaz, Kris Bubic, Edgardo Henriquez
Just like 2025, this is where things get dicey. The Dodgers' bullpen isn't quite as banged up or as unreliable as they were last year, but they're not the air-tight, bulletproof coterie that their combined salaries suggest they should be. Henriquez will be coming straight off of the IL to rejoin the team in the NLDS, and Díaz, Sasaki, and Scott are all woefully unpredictable.
There is some thought that the Dodgers might carry eight relievers instead of nine, to free up a spot on the position player side for a guy like Kim. In this scenario, we'll stick with them taking nine. If not, Bubic is the most obvious cut. Last one in, first one out.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Max Muncy Reveals the Dodgers' Strategy to 'Keep the Switch Flipped' for October
item.dc:creator: Cameron Kiszla
item.description: Max Muncy is no stranger to postseason baseball, but he said it still fires him up. The longtime Los Angeles Dodger returned to his All-Star form this season, but he knows October is where you prove your worth. On Tuesday, he revealed what he and the team are doing to prepare for a run at a third straight World Series title. What are the Dodgers doing to get ready for the playoffs? As the Dodgers wait to find out who they’ll be facing in the National League Division Series, the players are worki
item.content:encoded:
Max Muncy is no stranger to postseason baseball, but he said it still fires him up.
The longtime Los Angeles Dodger returned to his All-Star form this season, but he knows October is where you prove your worth.
On Tuesday, he revealed what he and the team are doing to prepare for a run at a third straight World Series title.
What are the Dodgers doing to get ready for the playoffs?
As the Dodgers wait to find out who they’ll be facing in the National League Division Series, the players are working to stay ready and are strengthening their bond ahead of a grueling October.
“We’re trying to focus on ourselves getting ready this week,” he said via Zoom.
The way Muncy described the team’s strategy was something akin to the saying “if you stay ready, you don’t have to get ready.”
Similar to what the team did in 2024, the Dodgers still gather at the stadium daily, even without games to play.
It comes at a cost to players’ personal lives and time with their families, but Muncy argued that it’s necessary for the nature of playoff baseball.
Whereas teams with a bye might be more rested, they also are “going to be facing a team that’s already been through the fire.”
“It’s hard to go from being in an at-home setting to find trying to find a way to flip the switch,” he said. “And so the best way for us to do that was you get everyone together, you keep them at the field, you find a way to not let that switch ever be flipped off. That was something that I thought we did a really good job of in ’24 and we’re going to try to do it again this year.”
It also helps the Dodgers continue to build team chemistry, as “the postseason is when you’re going to come together,” he said.
That cohesiveness will be key when the level of competition is this high.
Dodgers expect to get everyone’s best
The Dodgers have struggled against some of the top teams in baseball this year, but Muncy said every opponent is difficult.
“This is the big leagues. These are the best players in the world,” he said.
Given that, he’s not worried about the level of competition changing in the playoffs, pointing to multiple examples of one team dominating another in the regular season only for the tables to be flipped come October.
“I know there’s things you look at on paper where you say, ‘this is a good matchup,’ but in October, it really doesn’t matter,” he said.
All that does matter is what happens on the field, and on Saturday, we’ll find out.
Do you like Max Muncy’s mindset heading into the playoffs?
